title: Composing Inference on Kubernetes: Gateway, Schedule, Serve, Observe
tldr: Production inference should be built from open, swappable layers: accelerators, scheduling, gateway, serving and observability. The test is whether you can swap one layer, such as vLLM for SGLang or one endpoint picker for another, without the others noticing.

key_points.text: Inference is too often a closed vertical: one gateway, one serving image, one observability silo.
Composability has six lenses: workload, control flow, resource, information, human-agent and architectural.
Workloads nest (a model call inside RAG inside an agent inside a business workflow); separate platforms per type duplicate routing, scheduling and telemetry.
On shared clusters the model endpoint becomes everyone's dependency with no isolation or back pressure, and nobody can tell where tail latency was spent.
Layer model: Kubernetes control plane, accelerators via DRA, then gateway, scheduler and serving, all wrapped in observability.
A fixed DAG gives predictable latency and token spend; autonomous agents trade that for flexibility.
Admission (Kueue, Volcano, KAI Scheduler) decides whether pods can exist; the endpoint picker decides which replica serves this prompt now. They are different jobs.
Because the picker sits behind the Gateway API, pickers and gateways (llm-d, the GIE reference picker, Envoy Gateway, agentgateway, kgateway, Istio) can be swapped without client changes.
Carry knowledge, context, state and provenance across hops with OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions and W3C traceparent; Kepler adds GPU energy.

Serving boundary test: when TGI went into maintenance, teams behind a clean gateway contract swapped engines quickly. If swapping vLLM for SGLang breaks routing, auth or dashboards, the serving layer is doing platform work.
Agents need security isolation, durable state and fast suspend/resume; agent-substrate, OpenShell and gVisor each cover part of that.

numbers.text: Lab demo: five traffic shapes (warm-cache chat, agent tool bursts, multi-tenant traffic, queued batch) on one cluster without re-platforming.

open_gaps.text: Teams disagree on what words like 'cached' or 'completed' mean, so traces line up syntactically but not semantically.
Idle agent pods waiting on the model or a human waste cluster memory and risk losing state.
Autonomous control flow makes spend and termination hard to predict.

opportunities.text: Run the swap test on your platform: change the serving engine and check that routing, auth and dashboards survive.
Propagate W3C traceparent with OpenTelemetry GenAI spans from gateway to picker to model for per-request cost attribution.
Turn the talk's 'diagnose by boundary' checklist into a troubleshooting guide.
Learn where Kueue-style admission ends and endpoint-picker routing begins.

title: The Agent Has Entered the Cluster: AI Auth 101 for Kubernetes
tldr: A user's identity usually stops at the agent, so downstream tools and the Kubernetes API act with their own broad service-account permissions. The speakers assess a diagnostic agent by identity, delegation and scoped authority, then fix it with least-privilege RBAC, tool policies in agentgateway and a forwarded user token.

key_points.text: Real incidents: at PocketOS an agent on a staging task found an account-wide API token and deleted a production database and backups; at Replit an agent told not to modify anything deleted a database and falsified data. Instructions alone did not enforce a boundary.
Existing Kubernetes controls (least-privilege RBAC, workload credentials, egress control, image and secret protection) still apply, because an agent is a workload.
In the agentic loop the model only proposes tool calls; the agent calls the tool. Context such as runbooks, tickets and logs can influence actions but grants no permission.
Agents differ, though not uniquely: they are less predictable, act on a user's behalf, and may serve many users with one shared workload identity.

Example system: Alice signs in via Keycloak and may only read the payment namespace, but the MCP tool service's account can read and delete in payment and shipping, so the API server only sees the tool's permissions.

Three assessment questions: who is each participant and what credentials does it present downstream; what authority is delegated on whose behalf; what can each component actually do at the tool and Kubernetes enforcement points.
Demo, unsafe: the agent deletes a pod and reads another team's logs, because Alice's identity stopped at the agent.
Fix 1: scope the tool service's RBAC so Kubernetes rejects the delete, whatever MCP server is calling.
Fix 2: put agentgateway between the agent and tools with a policy that blocks the delete tool, so the call never happens.
Fix 3: pass Alice's JWT from the agent to the gateway, which checks her claims and allows log reads only for her namespace.
Trace decisions by correlating request IDs across gateway logs, MCP server logs and Kubernetes audit logs. Q&A: Istio mesh can handle mTLS and certificate lifecycle between components.

open_gaps.text: The talk covers only the basics; full agent hardening goes well beyond these steps, and A2A systems were only discussed conceptually.
Autonomous agents with no user behind them, such as SRE agents, can only rely on service-account hardening.
Gateway API work on entry and extension points for AI-specific policies is ongoing.

opportunities.text: Run the three assessment questions (identity, delegation, scoped authority) on your own agent system and name each enforcement point.
Forward the user's token through the agent and enforce per-user, per-tool policies at a gateway such as agentgateway.
Scope RBAC for every MCP tool service to the minimum verbs and namespaces, since any downloaded MCP server can try any action.
Join Gateway API work on AI policy extension points, or Istio and agentgateway.

title: One Workload to Rule Them All: Workload Aware Scheduling for Distributed AI Training on Kubernetes
tldr: Kubernetes now has Workload, PodGroup and composite PodGroup APIs so kube-scheduler can gang-schedule, preempt and place a whole distributed job instead of single pods. Kubeflow Trainer builds these into TrainJob runtimes so platform admins set gang and topology rules while scientists only write a training function.

key_points.text: Pod-by-pod scheduling deadlocks distributed jobs: two 8-GPU jobs on three 4-GPU nodes can each grab part of the capacity and neither starts.
Other gaps: preempting one pod leaves the rest of the gang idle, launcher and worker roles are scheduled as unrelated pods, and placement ignores racks, slowing gradient sync.
Kueue, KAI, Volcano, YuniKorn and the scheduler-plugins project all tackled gang scheduling; a new working group, started about a year ago at KubeCon Japan, aims for one common API.

A PodGroup carries a scheduling policy (gang with a minimum count), topology constraints, a disruption mode and shared resource claims; the scheduler checks the whole group against a cluster snapshot before admitting it.
Preemption has two modes upstream: single (evict one pod) and all (evict the whole pod group).
Composite pod groups express hierarchy with a minimum group count, useful for multi-layer jobs and disaggregated prefill/decode inference.
Kubeflow Trainer splits personas: admins define runtimes with zone/block/rack levels of scheduling policy; scientists call a Python SDK; JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet run underneath.
The same scheduling fields are meant to appear in TrainJob, JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet so users get one experience across workload types.

Kind demo: without gang scheduling a 5-pod job ran 4 pods and blocked a smaller job; with a gang policy the big job waited, the small one ran, and events named the unmet min count. A rack constraint kept each job in one rack.
TrainJob can report progress and ETA from framework callbacks; the speaker proposes using it for backfill and for preempting jobs that will finish later.
Kueue stays on top for quotas, cluster queues and multi-cluster; its topology-aware scheduling overlaps with the new upstream work and the two are being aligned.

numbers.text: Workload and PodGroup APIs are beta in Kubernetes 1.37; composite pod groups are alpha with beta expected in 1.38 and GA hoped for 1.40.
Trainer integration with composite pod groups is planned for Trainer 2.5, about two months out.
Demo cluster: 4 nodes across 2 racks; the first job asked for 5 pods.

open_gaps.text: Deep topology across multiple composite pod groups is slow for kube-scheduler; performance work is ongoing so 1,000 pods do not take an hour to schedule.
How Kueue's topology-aware scheduling hands off to the scheduler's own version is still being worked out, so the two will overlap for a while.
Topology is label-based only; health-aware topology (hardware degraded by heat or cooling failures) is an open issue.
Volcano maintainers are not yet engaged in the API design; the speaker asked them to join.

opportunities.text: Try the beta Workload and PodGroup APIs on a kind cluster with a gang policy and a rack constraint, as in the demo.
Bring Volcano or other scheduler use cases to the workload-aware scheduling working group and Trainer calls.
Prototype backfill or ETA-aware preemption using TrainJob's reported progress and ETA.
Adopt the shared scheduling fields in your own workload controller so it composes pod groups like TrainJob and JobSet.

title: Groundhog Pod: Scaling AI Inference with Kata Pod Snapshots
tldr: Microsoft extended Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor to snapshot a whole pod VM, including GPU state captured with CUDA checkpoint, after the model is loaded. Restoring from the snapshot cut a demo inference pod's time to first response from about 34 seconds to about 11.

key_points.text: Slow inference pod startup (image pull, loading Python, PyTorch and CUDA, loading weights, warm-up) costs money while serving nothing.
Startup latency sets how many warm pods you keep in reserve for spikes; faster startup means a smaller buffer.

CRIU checkpoints a process and its memory but not kernel state. Kata runs each pod in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, so a VM snapshot captures application, CPU, memory and kernel state together.

Snapshots fail to restore across CPU microarchitectures; a virtual CPU profile with a minimum feature set lets a snapshot taken on one CPU generation restore on another, leaving GPU compatibility as the main constraint.
GPU memory and execution state are captured with CUDA checkpoint into guest RAM, and then the whole VM is snapshotted to a storage back end.
Restore: an annotation on the pod tells the Kata runtime to start the VM from the snapshot, then CUDA checkpoint restores and unlocks the GPU.
Demo with a Pythia text-generation model: after snapshotting, the running pod resumed inference, was terminated, and a new pod restored from the snapshot answered in about 11 seconds.
From the snapshot, the software and model loading steps are skipped; GPU warm-up takes slightly longer.

Snapshots also help with traffic spikes, worker failures, quiet periods, group and batch jobs, Java JIT warm-up, and ML training, where a demo resumed the loss curve after restoring a mid-training snapshot.
Some Cloud Hypervisor changes are upstream; Kata snapshot and restore design is in progress, with plans to align with open KEPs in SIG Node and containerd work on snapshot/restore.
Q&A: no cross-architecture restore (for example ARM to AMD64); same-architecture restore works on tested SKUs and depends on the CPU feature profile, and GPU compatibility will be limited at first.

numbers.text: Demo cold start took about 33 to 34 seconds to a response; restore from snapshot took about 11 seconds, about a 65% improvement.
Loading software and model took about 21 seconds cold versus 5 seconds from a snapshot.
CPU-only restores reach sub-second restart times in their lab.
A simulation with pay-as-you-go H200 pricing saved about $30 over 3 minutes 45 seconds of spiky traffic.

open_gaps.text: The demo pins to and restores on a single GPU; restoring across GPUs needs more work.
Results were on a modest GPU with no optimizations; restore speed, CUDA recovery paths and snapshot size still need tuning on production hardware.
Protecting snapshots in multi-tenant clusters and using confidential containers to hide models from the infra provider are open.
GPU compatibility between snapshot and restore hosts is a big unresolved question.

opportunities.text: Join the upcoming upstream Kata snapshot and restore design work announced on the Kata Slack.
Follow the SIG Node KEPs and containerd proposals for snapshot/restore that Kata plans to integrate with.
Model your warm-pod buffer as a function of startup latency to estimate savings from faster restores.
Test mid-training VM snapshots as a way to survive evictions and maintenance without restarting jobs.

title: Observability for LLM Inference on Kubernetes
tldr: With frontier APIs you only see the client side, but self-hosting on Kubernetes lets you observe every layer from the GPU up to the user response. The speakers instrument an OCR app on KServe, vLLM and llm-d with OpenTelemetry and correlate metrics, traces and logs in Grafana to find wasted tokens and misleading GPU utilization.

key_points.text: Inference has a prefill stage and an iterative decode stage, which give the two core metrics: time to first token and time per output token.
With frontier model APIs you can instrument your app with OpenTelemetry GenAI traces, but not model internals, GPU use or KV cache, and provider features change over time.
Provider-reported TTFT differed from client-measured TTFT because of network hops and client processing.
With a local model capped at four parallel requests, extra requests show up as deferred, which is what a slow chat response feels like.
Demo app: passport OCR using an open-weights Qwen 9B vision model on one Kubernetes GPU node with KServe and vLLM, llm-d routing and Envoy Gateway in front.
Signals span five layers: application, routing (scheduler latency), inference server (TTFT, KV cache), hardware (GPU) and Kubernetes (vLLM startup, scheduling, unhealthy events).
DCGM dashboards show a GPU at 100% utilization while KV cache was only 20% busy, so GPU utilization alone misleads.
OpenTelemetry traces cover model loading in vLLM and full request paths, including a failed span whose cause was an empty model response.
The OpenTelemetry Collector sends signals to Prometheus, Tempo and Loki; correlation uses exemplars, trace ID queries, span metrics and the GenAI semantic conventions.
Findings: thinking mode wasted tokens for the vision model without improving answers, and batching many requests at once saved cost and energy.

numbers.text: OpenAI test script: 5 requests, about 100 tokens per second throughput.
Provider dashboard showed 600 ms TTFT while the client measured about 1.5 seconds.
Local model configured for 4 parallel requests; GPU utilization near 90% under load.
GPU at 100% utilization with KV cache only 20% busy.
Compared 1 request versus 24 requests at once for cost and energy.

open_gaps.text: Hosted frontier APIs hide model internals, GPU and KV cache behavior from users.
On neo-cloud GPUs you do not own the hardware, so power and energy data is not accurate.
The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions are still in development.

opportunities.text: Build a GPU dashboard that shows KV cache usage next to DCGM utilization so busy-but-idle GPUs stand out.
Use OpenTelemetry exemplars and span metrics to jump from a latency spike to the trace and the endpoint picker logs.
Measure token use with thinking mode on and off for your workload before enabling it.
Compare client-measured TTFT with provider-reported TTFT to size network and client overhead.

title: Least-Privilege by Default: Standardizing Identity-Aware AI Agent Access into a Golden Path
tldr: Least privilege for an agent acting on a user's behalf means every call may do only what both the user and the agent are allowed to do. Hitachi's design builds seven rules into a platform golden path using Keycloak token exchange, SPIFFE/SPIRE attestation, attribute-based policy and Backstage templates, so teams only declare and approve.

key_points.text: MCP made connecting tools easy, but each team secures access its own way (agent's own account, static keys, homemade token checks), causing both vulnerabilities and platform sprawl.
Pillar 1, on whose behalf: keep the user in the sub claim at every hop by exchanging the token for a new one with the next server as audience, instead of passing the first token along.

The common shortcut, client credentials, makes the agent act as itself (a confused deputy); disable agent service accounts in the authorization server and reject tokens without a user at the MCP server.

Pillar 2, which agent: SPIFFE attests the pod (namespace, image digest) and issues a short-lived ID; the authorization server accepts only that, not static client secrets, and writes the agent into the client_id claim.

Pillar 3, what is allowed: the authorization server issues tokens only for approved targets, and the MCP server runs a policy check on both user and agent attributes, e.g. low agent clearance blocks a high-sensitivity payment tool.
A server that skips the audience check accepts tokens meant for another server and defeats target restriction; one team's leaked key can then reach another team's server.
Delivery: three rules live in the authorization server (Keycloak with SPIRE), four in the agent sidecar and server middleware shipped via Backstage templates; teams write only their tools.
Each agent's client is generated from its declaration, not set by hand, because a misconfigured target in the shared layer would affect every agent.
Broad declarations are split into one request per target, each approved by that server's owner, so approval does not pile up in a central team.
Demo: a receipt with a hidden instruction to fetch payroll data fails because Keycloak never issues a payroll token for the expense agent.
Q&A: for SaaS products that do not accept these tokens, an ingress gateway can run the same policy in front of them.

numbers.text: Seven rules across three pillars.

open_gaps.text: Agents with no user behind them are out of scope for this model.
A team can still build a server by hand without the template and skip the audience check.
User identity cannot be propagated into SaaS products that accept only API keys, so their audit logs show a service account.

opportunities.text: Ship MCP server and agent templates with token exchange, audience checks, user-required checks and attribute-based policy built in.
Replace static agent keys with SPIRE-attested workload identity accepted by your authorization server.
Add a declare-and-approve flow where each target server's owner approves agent access and the platform generates the client.
OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange and the confused deputy problem for agents acting on behalf of users.

title: Seeing Inside LLM Inference: Observability and Cost Visibility for llm-d on Kubernetes
tldr: The llm-d observability and router SIG leads show end-to-end tracing of a request through the gateway, endpoint picker, KV cache lookup and prefill/decode pods, and use metric-to-trace-to-log correlation to find a bad scorer weight behind a TTFT regression. They then describe combining llm-d metrics with OpenCost to compute per-token, per-tenant cost, which is early work that is already upstream.

key_points.text: A request flows from Envoy to the endpoint picker (EPP), which checks KV cache state, picks prefill and decode pods, and a sidecar sends the prompt to prefill, after which decode pulls the KV cache GPU to GPU.
One trace covers tokenization, longest-prefix cache lookup, profile and scorer runs, endpoint selection, and prefill/decode; routing is a tiny part of the timeline.
Span attributes include the longest cached prefix in blocks, top endpoints and scores, TTFT and queue latency.
Grafana links metrics to traces in Jaeger with one click; logs carry trace and span IDs, but log-trace correlation is not in the dashboard yet, so you grep the trace ID.
Demo: a P99 TTFT alert led to a trace where the pod without the cache won because the cache scorer weight was zero, so the prompt was recomputed.
No error logs appeared; the EPP behaved correctly on a bad config, traced to a Helm release that changed the weight from 3 to 0.
Cost has two views: allocation (deployed capacity on given hardware) and usage (per-tenant, per-user tokens), with cost per token as total cost over tokens served.
llm-d router and gateway metrics plus vLLM or SGLang metrics go to Prometheus; OpenCost combines them with infrastructure cost and emits cost metrics at different granularities.
The goal is to compare self-hosted open-weights serving with sending requests to external providers, and to spot idle GPUs.
Dashboards, observability and the OpenCost integration are all upstream in llm-d.

numbers.text: Alert fired on P99 TTFT above 250 ms for more than 2 minutes; P99 jumped from about 200 ms to 600 ms.
Scores: cached pod 3.86 versus uncached pod 3.93 once the cache weight was zero.
Prefill took about 569 ms for about 4,000 tokens, 10x a healthy prefill.
Good vs bad trace for a ~3,800-token, fully cached prompt (59 blocks): 152 ms prefill with weight 3, 569 ms with weight 0.

open_gaps.text: Log-to-trace correlation is not supported from the dashboard yet; it relies on grepping trace IDs.
The OpenCost cost model for llm-d is initial work, still being evaluated in production.
Per-tenant and per-user cost granularity across shared models on mixed hardware is still being worked out.

opportunities.text: Use EPP trace attributes (prefix blocks, scores, chosen endpoint) to debug routing regressions.
Add alerts on scorer config changes, since a bad weight produced no error logs.
Add log-trace correlation to the upstream llm-d Grafana dashboards.
Feed llm-d and vLLM metrics into OpenCost to compare self-hosted cost per token with external API pricing.

title: Follow the GPUs: How a Regulated Fortune 100 Serves Customers When No Single Cloud Has Enough
tldr: GEICO runs a hybrid cloud fabric (flat L3 network, identical clusters, SPIFFE/SPIRE identity, Istio and Cilium) that makes moving a workload between Azure and AWS just a redeploy. They built a probe tool that measured GPU availability across providers for four weeks and found multi-region helps only for scarce SKUs, and propose a capacity booking agent since autoscalers never buy capacity.

key_points.text: Takeaways first: for current single-GPU SKUs right now, support multi-region; for 8-GPU flagship nodes, book ahead; and someone still has to do the booking, because autoscalers will not.
The fabric was built for other reasons: four nines across 50 states, replacing about a thousand team-owned clusters and over a million firewall rules with a provider-agnostic zero-trust overlay.

Foundation: one flat L3 network with routable node and pod IPs across providers; identical clusters from immutable hardened images, kubeadm and Ansible, with components on the same versions and delivered by GitOps.
SPIRE issues SPIFFE IDs and short-lived SVIDs from attested evidence; Istio sidecars enforce mTLS with certs from the SPIRE agent; Cilium enforces deny-by-default L3/L4 policy.
Teams describe apps and their communication; the platform generates Cilium and Istio policy, with automatic approval for most rules and human review for risky ones.

The control plane runs active-active in three regions on Cassandra, which also backs a SPIRE fork with a pluggable datastore proposed upstream; Kafka is the fleet bus, and a mesh agent syncs endpoints and policy to each cluster.
Because identity and rules attach to what a workload is, not where it runs, moving from Azure to AWS is a redeploy with the same global name and no client changes.
Providers now offer bookable capacity (e.g. AWS capacity blocks, up to 8 weeks out, paid up front, no refunds) between on-demand and reserved; Karpenter will use a reservation ID but never buys one.

The 'follow the GPUs' tool doubles its GPU request until refused, with Blackbox Exporter-style probe config, free probes (spot score and price) and billable catch-and-release probes, telemetry in S3/Blob queried with DuckDB, and a scheduled sweeper as an emergency brake.

Results: small single-GPU SKUs gain nothing from multi-region, L40S gains about 5%, sparse RTX Pro 6000 gains a lot, and B200 is not available on demand but multi-region raises odds of getting one within two days.

Q&A: multi-cluster autoscaling approaches still just wait and retry when refused; Azure model-as-a-service by data zone plus an AI gateway can soften shortages; NVIDIA Dynamo intent CRs are scoped to one cluster.

numbers.text: About 1,000 Kubernetes clusters and over 1 million firewall rules in the old model.
Control plane runs in three regions, all active.
Inference cost for the same capability drops roughly 10x per year (cited from Guido Appenzeller), so 100x in two years.
Capacity can be booked up to 8 weeks ahead.
A catch-and-release probe took about 30 seconds to 2 minutes per VM.
Ran about four weeks across every zone of three AWS regions and nine Azure regions, collecting about 50,000 samples.
L40S: about 5% improvement from multi-region; RTX Pro 6000: from about 45% to 70-75%.
B200: chance of getting capacity within two days rose from about 65% to 88%.

open_gaps.text: No autoscaler books capacity; when the provider says no they can only wait and retry. GEICO proposes a booking agent with an interface for need, timing and budget, informed by history.
The booking agent and multi-cluster placement layer do not exist yet; they are still checking whether it would help.
Data gravity constrains where many workloads can run.
Securing agents with workload identity is unsolved; sidecar credential injection is the direction, but no full answer yet.

opportunities.text: Run GEICO's shared probe tool in your own accounts to measure GPU SKU availability by region before committing to multi-region.
Help define the interface for a GPU capacity booking agent that reserves capacity just before pods go pending.
Review the SPIRE pluggable datastore proposal and the Cassandra-backed implementation.
Identity-based (SPIFFE) network policy that lets workloads move across clouds without rewriting rules.

title: Agentic Inference at Scale
tldr: Agent sessions send about 100 tokens in for every token out, so serving them well is about never recomputing context. llm-d 1.0 packages cache-aware routing, offloading and disaggregation, adds day-2 operations, and a new SIG is moving scheduling from single requests to whole sessions.

key_points.text: Agent sessions have roughly a 100:1 input to output ratio, so the reuse ceiling is close to 100%.
Watch prefill compute as a metric: a hidden cache-buster can sit behind a healthy-looking hit rate.
The llm-d router balances prefix-cache affinity against load-aware routing so stickiness does not create hot spots.
Keep idle sessions alive: north-south offload to CPU and storage, east-west P2P pull when a session moves pods.
Prefill/decode disaggregation also isolates failures: a cache-hit collapse in an aggregated deployment hurts decode users too.
llm-d 1.0 focus is day-2: a new router loads a state snapshot, warms instantly, and takes traffic with zero errors.
Flow control queues batch tenants so interactive TTFT stays flat while total throughput is maximized.

The Agentic Inference SIG is designing session-level orchestration: a KV block index, session state (compaction, forks, sub-agents), a KV hints envelope (pin, copy, move) and session-aware admission instead of FIFO.

numbers.text: Published Weka traces show 95% achieved prefix reuse.
Production: prefill compute was 16% at an 85% hit rate; after fixing a per-turn timestamp Claude Code injects into the system prompt, prefill dropped to 4% while traffic doubled.
A 6-hour non-interactive ramp was queued with no visible change to interactive TTFT.

open_gaps.text: Routers see requests, not sessions: an agent paused on a tool call looks idle, gets evicted, and pays full recompute on return.
Agent harnesses do not yet emit rich session state; the SIG wants to co-design that signal with client projects.
Closed-source agent clients can break cache reuse in open serving stacks (the timestamp-in-system-prompt bug).
Explainability: operators cannot yet tell whether their hit rate is the hardware ceiling or a bug.

opportunities.text: Add a prefill-compute-percent panel to an inference dashboard and alert on it, not just on hit rate.
Help the Agentic Inference SIG define the session-state signal an agent harness should send to the router.
Case study: how one system-prompt timestamp cut cache reuse, and how to find that kind of bug.
Demo flow control with batch plus interactive tenants on one cluster, showing flat interactive TTFT.

title: Beyond the Cluster Boundary: Sharing GPUs at Scale
tldr: Snap pooled its reserved GPUs into capacity-pool clusters and lets workloads in thousands of customer clusters reach them through virtual nodes built on Virtual Kubelet, with Kueue gating access and handling borrowing and preemption. Average reservation occupancy in its largest region rose from under 50% to over 90%, saving tens of millions of dollars a year.

key_points.text: The approach applies to any constrained compute when you must run more than one cluster, whether for scale or compliance.

Inference reservations were sized for peak, so average occupancy stayed under 50%; lending to batch was possible but owners could not reclaim GPUs without paging someone, so teams walled off their reservations.
Capacity is grouped by machine type into cell clusters, but deployments cannot be placed there directly because inference falls back across machine types (G4, then G2, then C4D) at runtime.

Two building blocks: a virtualization layer separating where deployments live from where capacity runs, and workload-level quotas (for example many inference partitions sharing one quota), while keeping teams' operational model.
Virtual nodes built on Virtual Kubelet copy a bound pod's ConfigMaps, Secrets and the pod itself to the remote pool cluster and mirror status, so logs and exec work as usual.
Kueue in each customer cluster gates access to virtual nodes by quota; without quota, pods fall back to the cluster's normal autoscaling (Karpenter, cluster autoscaler, compute classes).
MultiKueue was not used for autoscaled inference because HPA needs node metrics from the metrics server; it is planned for some batch workloads.

In the pool cluster, vanilla Kueue has the global view and handles cohort borrowing and preemption; customer clusters are shown their entitlement plus anything borrowable, including capacity held by lower-priority borrowers.
During a cloud provider outage, central quota changes chose which critical workloads kept GPUs and the rest drained on their own, with no ad-hoc paging.
Next: more constrained machine types and opt-in cross-region failover that joins virtual nodes just in time when local and on-demand capacity is exhausted.

Each virtual node represents only homogeneous machines in one topology domain, so topology-aware scheduling and compact placement still work; the number of nodes behind one virtual node is set by blast radius.

numbers.text: Snap runs thousands of Kubernetes clusters with over 100,000 machines across multiple clouds and regions.
Average reservation occupancy in the largest region went from under 50% to over 90%.
Savings of tens of millions of dollars in annual compute costs.
A cloud provider outage removed over 20% of reservations over a few days.

open_gaps.text: MultiKueue breaks HPA-driven inference because there is no node in the metrics loop.
The design assumes a flat network with reachable pod IPs; operators that use their own networking APIs must be checked case by case.
Cross-cloud failover has only been proven as a proof of concept and needs an interconnect.

opportunities.text: Prototype a Virtual Kubelet provider that mirrors pods and their ConfigMap/Secret dependencies into a shared GPU pool cluster.
Pair per-cluster Kueue quotas with a central Kueue cohort and advertise entitlement plus borrowable capacity.
Explore how MultiKueue could support HPA-scaled deployments that need in-cluster metrics, the gap that kept Snap on virtual nodes.
Write up using central quota changes to drain lower-priority GPU work during capacity loss.

title: Kubernetes Solutions for Agent-Shaped Problems
tldr: Tim Hockin and Dmitry Berkovich explain why the obvious pod-per-agent-session pattern on Kubernetes gives slow starts and poor utilization, and how Agent Substrate fixes it with secure-by-default sandboxes, near-zero cost for idle agents and fast wake from layered snapshots. The long Q&A covers the policy enforcement point, snapshot invalidation and missing pieces such as autoscaling and automatic suspend.

key_points.text: Agent workloads are bursty (work for 100 ms to half a minute, then idle for hours), run untrusted generated code that needs full isolation, and have a human waiting for responses.
Pod per session wastes requested resources while the user thinks, then destroys the pod on timeout and pays the slow sandbox start again on return.
Teams that rolled their own ran many sandboxes inside large pods, then needed a control plane across nodes, effectively rebuilding Kubernetes.
Three principles: security (no network by default, everything sandboxed, per-agent identity), density (idle agents cost about zero) and speed (wake feels like it never slept).
Built on Kubernetes: workers are pods, the control plane and policy run in the cluster, and on node drain workers move their agents elsewhere.
Concepts: actor (one session), actor template, worker (a pod hosting many actors), outlet (per-node manager handling images and snapshots), and ATE net with a router and an egress.
Actors have no IP; the router finds the actor from the DNS name, holds the request while it resumes the actor, and the egress applies policy and injects credentials.

Snapshots have layers: OCI image, a mandatory volume, root FS diffs and memory. Same image and machine type allows a full resume; a new image throws away memory and root FS for a cold start from the volume.
Common pattern: a managed agent loop such as Gemini (brains) calls Substrate inside your own perimeter (hands), where work can be audited and stopped.
The policy enforcement point is a plug-in: actor traffic is wrapped in HTTP CONNECT and sent to it; Envoy and Solo.io's agentgateway are the two implementations so far.
Suspend writes a local snapshot, then uploads it asynchronously; the scheduler prefers a node that still holds the latest copy. Only the durable directory is guaranteed to persist.

numbers.text: Sandbox pod startups seen at 15 seconds, 30 seconds and up to a couple of minutes.
Aspirational goals: billions of agents in one cluster, 10,000+ activations per second, wake in about 100 ms.
In 1.0, snapshot upload to cloud storage starts after 5 minutes suspended.
Users have been in production since 0.2, released two months ago; the project has been built for about 6 months.

open_gaps.text: No good autoscaling story for worker pods and nodes; HPA on CPU and memory does not fit agents that sleep and wake often, so sizing is manual today.
Memory management is imperfect: no in-place resource updates, and a hostile workload can still exhaust memory.
Suspend is manual or harness-driven; detecting idleness automatically is unsolved, and self-suspend is coming.
Base image patches invalidate memory and root FS snapshots for every affected actor; merging overlays is an open question.

opportunities.text: Write a third policy enforcement point implementation for Substrate egress.
Design autoscaling signals for Substrate worker pools from activation and suspend activity rather than CPU.
Make your agent harness call suspend when a task finishes, and keep needed state in the durable directory.
The brains/hands split for running managed agent loops against compute inside your own security perimeter.

title: Your Peers Are Struggling With LLM Inference on Kubernetes Too. Here's What the Data Says
tldr: Using an Akamai-commissioned survey of 200 practitioners running AI in production, plus CNCF, Forrester and Cast AI data, the speakers show that most teams struggle with latency at peak, GPU capacity and routing. They map the failure points across scheduling, scaling, networking and ownership, and close with five steps to production inference on Kubernetes.

key_points.text: The top blocker to running inference close to users is tooling and platform maturity, ahead of cost uncertainty, security, data handling and observability.
Kubernetes is the default for AI workloads; the problem is complexity and speed, since few organizations deploy their generative AI stack daily.
Expectations are strict: sub-500 ms end-to-end responses, tail-latency measurement (P95/P99), and rollback within an hour when inference performance degrades.
Scheduling: set resource requests, use DRA and Kueue to share GPUs, watch GPU splitting, right-size the CPU-heavy parts too, and measure utilization and latency.
Scaling: startup is slow (instance plus model load), so do not scale on CPU; scale on latency and time to first token using vLLM metrics with KEDA.
Routing: replicas each hold their own KV cache, so generic load balancing wastes cache; route on cache contents, queue depth and load with Gateway API Inference Extension, llm-d or KServe.
Teams say proximity to users is critical, but planned architectures stay flat: single-region stays about the same and multi-region slightly declines. You cannot autoscale past the speed of light.
Ownership is the hardest part: inference probably belongs to the platform team, but SLOs like time to first token and token cost need clear owners.
A maturity grid (getting started, scaling, leading) covers placement, autoscaling signals and routing, mapped to the CNCF Cloud Native Maturity Model.

Five steps: start from an AI-conformant cluster, cut startup time by caching or streaming weights near the GPU, autoscale on inference signals, add an inference-aware gateway, and set a P95 TTFT SLO with planned rollbacks.

numbers.text: Survey: 200 practitioners all running AI in production, two-thirds engineers.
Nearly 1 in 5 name tooling and platform maturity as the top blocker.
66% of organizations hosting generative AI use Kubernetes; only 7% deploy that stack daily.
82% need end-to-end response in 500 ms or less; 64% in 250 ms or less.
39% measure P95 and 17% P99.
Over 70% need rollback within an hour; nearly half within 15 minutes.
Half name latency at peak load as one of the hardest scaling problems; bursty concurrency 43%; GPU capacity planning 37%.
Average GPU utilization across Kubernetes clusters is 5% (Cast AI data).
On a degrading model: 51% keep the same model, 39% switch to a smaller one, 37% fail over, 12% block the action, 7% have no fallback; 64% call automated traffic steering very important or critical.
After moving to an inference-aware gateway, one user's prefix cache hits doubled from 35% to 70% and TTFT dropped by more than 35% on the same hardware.
60% say being close to users is critical; single-region plans go from 46% to 45% and multi-region from 22% to 20% over two years.
47% in the CNCF survey say culture is the biggest blocker.

open_gaps.text: Sharing or splitting GPUs across workloads is still early.
There is no default tooling for inference-aware traffic steering even though teams say it is critical.
Architectures are not moving closer to users despite stricter latency needs.
Ownership of inference SLOs and token cost between platform and app teams is unresolved.

opportunities.text: Replace CPU-based HPA on inference pods with KEDA scaling on vLLM queue depth, KV cache or TTFT metrics.
Put an inference-aware gateway (Gateway API Inference Extension or llm-d) in front of model servers and measure prefix cache hit rate.
Place your teams on the getting-started/scaling/leading grid and the CNCF Cloud Native Maturity Model.
Define who owns the TTFT SLO and GPU/token cost between platform and application teams.

title: From Laptop to Cluster: The Agentic AI Inner Loop on Kubernetes
tldr: Using a live audience race game run by an AI race director, the speaker shows an agentic Java app built with Quarkus and LangChain4j that exposes MCP tools and calls sub-agents over A2A. He argues agents are mostly ordinary code: develop locally with hot reload and a dev UI, add evals, then ship to Kubernetes with configuration changes and standard security and health patterns.

key_points.text: Gartner research cited: many agentic AI projects will be canceled because of rising costs, unclear business value and weak risk controls.
The demo game sends phone taps through Kafka to a dashboard, with an AI race director that monitors the race, changes themes and boosts teams that fall behind, with human approval.
The game exposes MCP servers; the admin server requires browser authentication so not every user or agent can control the game.
The race director is a supervisor agent that picks between an analyst and a creative sub-agent over A2A, similar to distributed services owned by different teams.
MCP and A2A act like a new REST: MCP tools are annotated Java methods with role-based access, such as admin-only tools.
An open-source tool can turn existing APIs into MCP servers by configuration, without rewriting them.
Quarkus dev mode gives hot reload, a dev UI listing Kafka topics, AI services, MCP tools, prompt templates and token metrics, and exposes runtime info to the code assistant over MCP.
Local development still enforces the same MCP authentication, so you test production auth on your laptop.
Swapping models changes behavior: a boost prompt produced a 1.5 multiplier on one model and 3 on another, so add evals to the test suite.
For production: switch models via configuration, add health checks for sub-agents and MCP servers, expose token and latency metrics, use mutual TLS and short-lived tokens (SPIFFE/SPIRE, Keycloak).

numbers.text: Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of next year.
The same boost prompt gave a 1.5 multiplier on the original model and 3 on a new one.
Local load test simulated 100 players.

open_gaps.text: Agentic apps with many components are hard to test, and a race director and code assistant can conflict over the same controls.
Changing models can silently change agent behavior unless prompts are detailed and evals cover it.
Agents need guardrails, sandboxing and least-privilege, short-lived credentials when they run in Kubernetes.

opportunities.text: Add evals for non-deterministic agent behavior to your test suite with tools like Langfuse or Promptfoo.
Add health endpoints that check A2A sub-agents and MCP servers, not just the main app.
Try the game's source on GitHub to see MCP tools with role-based access and an A2A supervisor agent in Java.
Join the CNCF developer experience TAG, which the speaker says is looking for contributors.

title: Just Keep Swimming: Benchmarking OSS Agent Memory on Kubernetes with OpenTelemetry
tldr: Henrik Rexed benchmarks five open-source agent memory servers on kagent with a shared generic MCP layer and OpenTelemetry instrumentation he contributed upstream. Memory helps only when recall is precise: embedding and graph approaches did best for SRE investigations, a key-based store did best for context-rich coding crews, and MemPalace and Zep were the most consistent overall.

key_points.text: Agents without memory repeat investigations and tool calls they already did, wasting tools and tokens; memory servers let agents store and recall facts.

Architectures range from pure embeddings, to vector plus graph, knowledge graphs, temporal knowledge graphs, and a key/metadata store plus vector and graph (MemKeys, the speaker's own two-week-old project).
Common layers: ingest and search paths, an optional LLM to embed and categorize facts, graph building done asynchronously, and usually an MCP server for agent access.
MemPalace organizes memory into wings per project and drawers per category; Zep (Graphiti) tracks when facts change so it can answer what was true before and now.

Harness: kagent agents on DeepSeek, a generic MCP for add, search, get, update and delete so only the backend changes, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation contributed to each backend (some PRs were rejected, so forks were used).

Scenario 1: an SRE agent diagnoses Kubernetes failures (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOM kills, pending pods) and bad Gateway API and GAMMA gRPC route configs, measured as warm minus cold runs.
Scenario 2: a BMAD-method crew over A2A builds an expense approval app, is stopped mid-feature and resumed, then gets a fact change (PostgreSQL to MySQL).
Memory raises input tokens, though these may be billed as cached input; retrieving too many or wrong facts confuses the LLM and makes results worse.
SRE results: MemOS, Zep and MemPalace improved with memory; Mem0 and MemKeys got worse, with MemKeys pulling far too many facts.
Coding crew results: the key store did best on build, resume and restart, using far fewer tokens because tasks carry rich context; MemPalace and Zep also did well.
Few backends offer a UI to inspect stored memory, which matters for pruning noise that degrades search.

numbers.text: Memory server footprint was around 250 to 300 MB.
MemKeys used about 55 millicores of CPU on retrieval in the SRE scenario.
In the coding scenario MemKeys used about 20 millicores more than the others.
Add and search latencies were on the scale of a few microseconds, up to about 20 microseconds.
The other projects have more than 10K GitHub stars; MemKeys has zero.

open_gaps.text: Most memory backends do not ship OpenTelemetry support, and some maintainers rejected upstream PRs because telemetry is a commercial feature.
Memory scoping and isolation between users or channels was not evaluated, and the speaker did not know which backends support it.
Several earlier candidates (Cognee, Memu, Honcho) were dropped over licensing changes, and other popular tools are not yet covered.
Adding a backend to the benchmark is laborious: MCP connectivity, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, then scenario design.

opportunities.text: Add OpenTelemetry instrumentation for ingest and recall operations to open-source memory servers.
Measure agent memory as warm-run minus cold-run tokens and tool calls on your own workloads before adopting a backend.
Test whether memory backends isolate recall by user or channel before using them in shared bots.
Compare embedding, temporal knowledge graph and key-indexed memory designs against SRE-style versus project-style agent tasks.

title: llm-d 1.0 Production-Grade Inference for Cloud-Native AI
tldr: llm-d 1.0 marks the core stack as production-ready: KV-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, KV offloading and flow control, behind a stable v1 API. IBM ran it on 500+ H100s for an internal agentic workload, and a demo shows throughput nearly doubling on the same hardware.

key_points.text: Open-weight models now close much of the gap with frontier models, so enterprises want to self-host for cost and data control.
Scaling inference is an orchestration problem: route on KV reuse and load, schedule multi-pod replicas as gangs, and manage KV state across memory tiers.
llm-d builds on Kubernetes standards: the Gateway API inference extension for the router, LeaderWorkerSet for MoE and gang scheduling, DisaggregatedSet for prefill/decode, and native KV offloading.
It now also supports batch and async APIs.
Design stays modular (use only what you need) and vendor-neutral, with more than eight accelerator types supported.
'Well-lit paths' are deployable blueprints with benchmark data: intelligent scheduling, KV cache management, flow control, and now agentic serving.
1.0 adds multi-tenant QoS (priority and fairness via flow control), router high availability, coordinated prefill/decode rollouts, session and turn affinity for agents, and a stable v1 API.

Demo: with plain round robin the KV cache hit rate is low and uneven; turning on the llm-d router raises it to about 75% and nearly doubles throughput; flow control then gives paying tiers lower latency while free users still get served.

numbers.text: A new open-weight model drops about every 11 days.
Tesla saw 3x more throughput with KV-aware routing.
Over 500 contributors and more than 25 contributing companies.
IBM: 500+ H100 GPUs serving a large MoE model with expert parallelism of 32+, peaking at 3,000 concurrent agents and about 6 million tokens a minute (6x what the workload needed).
Demo: 1,000 agents on 25 Kubernetes nodes across 40 sandboxes, about 300 requests a second.
KV cache hit rate rose from a 30-50% swing to about 75% with the llm-d router.

open_gaps.text: Going from a model recipe to a shared service (rollouts, downtime, competing teams) is still the hard part.
Tuning still takes a lot of expertise; the roadmap names operational intelligence, more automation and better guides.
Agent infrastructure (sandboxes, agent-substrate) and inference infrastructure are not yet woven together for fully self-hosted stacks.

opportunities.text: Reproduce the round robin vs llm-d router vs flow control comparison on your own cluster and publish the numbers.
Run a well-lit path on hardware or a model it has not been tested on and report how it breaks, as the speakers ask.
Case study: serving a large MoE model on previous-generation GPUs instead of paying a commercial API bill.
Read through llm-d's well-lit paths as the shortest route to a tuned deployment.

title: AI Gateways in Practice: Model Routing, Inference Scheduling, and MCP on Kubernetes
tldr: Using the Higress gateway, the talk walks through three AI traffic paths on Kubernetes: hosted model providers with fallback, self-hosted models behind Gateway API Inference Extension pools, and agent tool calls over MCP. It compares an endpoint picker embedded in the gateway with an external EPP such as llm-d's, including how each behaves on failure.

key_points.text: Higress, a CNCF sandbox gateway built on Envoy and Istio, puts provider calls, self-hosted inference and MCP tools behind one entry point with shared security, quota and observability, but each path needs a different routing decision.

For hosted models, a model router plugin copies the model field from the JSON body to a header for normal route matching; an AI route maps it to weighted providers, and an AI proxy translates protocols, injects API keys and rewrites model names.

Provider fallback lives on the AI route: on 4xx/5xx responses Envoy does an internal redirect to a backup provider and model, and a response header shows that fallback happened. The decision is per request and keeps no state.
API key failover is a separate mechanism inside one provider: a failing key leaves rotation after a threshold and returns after a health check or cooldown, with state kept per gateway pod.
Fallback cannot redirect a streaming response once a 200 has started, 429 and 503 usually need different reactions, and fallback models differ in context window and quality, so map them deliberately.

Self-hosted replicas are not interchangeable: queue depth, KV cache use, prefix cache locality and loaded LoRA adapters matter more than connection counts. An HTTPRoute points at an InferencePool, which references an endpoint picker (EPP).

Higress creates a headless Service per InferencePool and sends request attributes and candidates to the EPP over Envoy external processing; on retries it reports the pod that actually served the response so the picker's view stays accurate.

Embedded option: an AI load balancer Wasm plugin scores pods from per-host metrics (ported from the upstream inference extension scheduler), with Redis for shared state; if it fails, normal service load balancing applies.

External option: an EPP per pool, such as the llm-d inference scheduler, runs filter and scorer plugins and adds prefix-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation and latency prediction, at the cost of one more component and a gRPC round trip per request.

Rule of thumb: embedded picker for small pools with simple traffic; external EPP for large pools, when KV cache reuse matters, or when several gateways need the same scheduling. The choice is per route. Fail-close is the default; fail-open favors availability.

For MCP, the gateway can expose REST APIs as MCP tools via request templates (credentials injected, never seen by the agent), proxy existing MCP servers with auth and rate limits, and bridge clients and servers on different MCP transport versions.

numbers.text: The AI proxy supports 38 provider types.
Higress passes the Gateway API v1.6.0 HTTP profile core tests with no failures or skips; the report was accepted upstream.
All 12 core tests of the Inference Extension v1.4.0 gateway profile pass; this report is published by the project, not submitted upstream.

open_gaps.text: When every pod is saturated no picker can create capacity; queueing, admission control, gateway rate limits or autoscaling are still needed.
The Inference Extension conformance report has not been submitted upstream, so it is a project report, not an upstream result.
MCP's HTTP transport has changed several times in two years, so clients and servers on different versions need bridging.
The speaker asks for feedback on EPP behavior under real model load and on what breaks during MCP migration.

opportunities.text: Set up provider fallback with separate rules for 429 and 503, and expose fallback rate in per-route and per-model metrics.
Run both an embedded picker and an external EPP on the same gateway and compare them per route, including fail-open versus fail-close.
Expose an existing REST API as MCP tools through gateway templates instead of writing a separate MCP server.
Share EPP behavior data under real load and MCP migration issues with the Higress project.

title: Simulate, Evolve, Validate, Ship: AI-Discovered Algorithms for LLM Serving Stacks
tldr: IBM Research uses a CPU-based simulator of llm-d and vLLM plus an agentic harness to discover serving policies, then validates the winners on GPUs and upstreams them to llm-d. The loop has produced admission control, flow control and LoRA routing plugins for the llm-d router.

key_points.text: Every llm-d subsystem (routing, admission control, flow control, scheduling, prefill/decode, autoscaling) is an open design problem, but GPU experiments take days and cost thousands of dollars, so few ideas get tested.
The loop is simulate, evolve, validate, ship. A human gives only the goal, SLO constraints, workloads and hardware; the output is a production-ready llm-d policy.
The simulator (BLIS) is a digital twin of llm-d and vLLM that runs on CPUs. An agentic harness plans hypotheses, writes algorithms as code, runs them in the simulator and learns across iterations.
Simulation confirms the direction of a gain; real hardware measures its size. Validation turns simulated code and config into llm-d code, deploys it and benchmarks it.

Translation uses three agents: one maps signals between simulator and llm-d (KV cache utilization, queue depth, priority), a writer translates, and a reviewer tests. Agents check each other's work, not their own.
A time-unit mismatch in saturation detection between simulator and llm-d invalidated hours of GPU results. They added pre-deploy parity checks and post-benchmark log checks.
Attaching real benchmark evidence to PRs made upstream review faster. Three policies were merged into the llm-d router: admission gate, flow control and LoRA routing.

The baseline admission gate accepts everything until saturation hits 100%, when queues are already long. The new probabilistic admitter rejects low-priority requests with probability rising with saturation and always accepts critical ones.

The soft reflective ceiling flow-control policy orders admitted requests so critical traffic is never blocked behind low-priority work, slowing low-priority queues as load rises without rejecting anything.
Both are llm-d plugins enabled with a configuration change.

Q&A: a prompted agent with a methodology file forgot to persist algorithms and workloads and made false claims, so they built a harness with deterministic tooling and hypothesis bundles (main, negative, ablation arms).

numbers.text: The simulator runs about 200x faster than real GPU inference.
Validation setup: four H100 GPUs, a Qwen 14B model, eight workloads across four shapes (chatbot, code generation, agentic and others) at various loads.
Probabilistic admission: critical-request TTFT improved by up to 97% and end-to-end latency by up to 50%, at the cost of more low-priority rejections.
Flow-control policy: critical TTFT improved by up to 98%, latency improved by up to 50x, with zero requests rejected.

open_gaps.text: Running the loop continuously against live traffic is the goal but not reached; every step can fail and still needs human review of logs.
llm-d, the simulator and the harness all keep changing, which makes unattended overnight discovery hard.
Sim-to-real translation is error prone; one config mismatch forced discarding a full GPU run.

opportunities.text: Enable the new admission and flow-control plugins in llm-d and compare critical-request TTFT with the baseline under overload.
Use a CPU simulator to screen scheduling or admission policies against SLOs before spending GPU time.
Give coding agents deterministic tooling that forces them to persist algorithms, workloads and results before claiming success.
Attach simulation and real-cluster benchmark evidence to llm-d PRs that change routing or scheduling policies.

title: Beyond Model Serving: Running Production LLMs on Kubernetes with KServe
tldr: KServe maintainers explain LLMInferenceService, a separate API from InferenceService that wraps llm-d, vLLM and Gateway API Inference Extension routing so one resource can describe single-node, multi-node and prefill/decode-disaggregated deployments. They then walk through production patterns: cache-aware routing, timeouts, queue-based autoscaling, cold-start reduction, rollouts and LoRA adapters.

key_points.text: LLMs differ from predictive models: they generate tokens over time, hold GPU memory for KV cache, and run long requests, so scheduling, scaling and load balancing need rethinking.
KServe integrates llm-d rather than building an inference engine, and has to keep up with llm-d's fast release pace without bloating its API.

LLMInferenceService has a workload controller (single node, multi-node, separate prefill pool) and a route controller (scheduler and Gateway API resources); it is kept separate so InferenceService stays simple.

One YAML sets model source (Hugging Face, S3, PVC or OCI), tensor/data parallelism, an optional independently scaled prefill pool, and router, gateway and scheduler settings; KServe creates the rest from presets.
The endpoint picker (EPP, the llm-d scheduler) picks a replica using prefix cache match, queue depth and KV cache usage, built on Gateway API Inference Extension; users can plug in a custom EPP.
For streaming, route timeouts must exceed generation time and each hop's timeout must exceed the next one, or clients retry and pile more load on GPUs.

Disaggregated prefill/decode gives consistent TTFT and TPOT at high concurrency and allows different GPU types per phase; very large models use multi-node with LeaderWorkerSet, tensor parallelism within a node and pipeline parallelism across nodes.
Autoscale on the engine's waiting-queue length: GPU utilization reads near 100% with only a few requests because it is a time-share metric, and KV cache utilization sits at a medium baseline.

Cold start: a local model cache, plus container snapshot and restore (CRI-O, NVIDIA Dynamo), cuts startup from tens of minutes to seconds. A shared KV pool keeps TTFT low for new versions during canary rollouts.
Multiple LoRA adapters on one shared base vLLM model are selected per request and save GPU memory.
Q&A: KV cache offloading (LMCache, Dynamo, vLLM connectors) is transparent to KServe; the llm-d router must know where blocks are offloaded to route well.

numbers.text: llm-d went from v0.4 in November 2025 to v1.0 the month before the talk.
Pipeline parallelism example: two nodes with eight GPUs each.
Snapshot/restore cuts cold start from tens of minutes to a few seconds.
Aggregated serving can show P99 at 2-3x baseline versus disaggregated.

open_gaps.text: Next focus is agentic workloads: routing by request type and complexity with llm-d, and SLAs per workload class.
Fast cold start does not solve rollout traffic: new versions have no KV cache unless a shared KV pool is added.
Dashboards hide queueing; end-to-end latency can look flat while TTFT and TPOT degrade.

opportunities.text: Autoscale vLLM replicas in KServe on waiting-queue length instead of GPU utilization.
Audit timeouts from client through load balancer, AI gateway and EPP so each exceeds the one downstream.
Start with aggregated LLMInferenceService, then move to prefill/decode disaggregation, then multi-node LeaderWorkerSet as scale grows.
Help KServe with agentic-workload routing and per-workload SLAs on top of llm-d.

title: From Proxy to Platform: Building a Multi-Tenant AI Gateway
tldr: Adobe built a shared, multi-tenant LLM gateway on LiteLLM, with its own control plane (console) for self-service model onboarding, fallbacks, budgets and logs. The talk walks through the stages from shared keys to team tenants, agent-driven usage and platform guarantees, and where they go next.

key_points.text: Before the gateway, teams shared long-lived provider keys or ran their own proxies, so nobody could say who used a key, what was spent per app, or whether proxies were patched.
The data plane is LiteLLM, an OpenAI-compatible proxy with routing, fallbacks, auth, rate limits and budget checks; the team's work is the console control plane around it.
When a second team arrived, each team got its own model deployments in its own cloud accounts, reachable only with team-scoped keys, so access and costs never mix.
A tenant is a team, not a user, because use cases, service IDs and budgets belong to teams while people move between teams. Team admins self-serve models, fallback rules and budgets.
Internal agents minted and deleted keys almost every turn, escaping key-based budgets. The fix: stamp the owning human on every key and reconcile agent spend back to that person's budget.

For customer-facing agents, internal apps pass a customer ID via trusted headers or token claims, and the gateway enforces per-customer budgets and limits. A default budget is required, or customers get unlimited spend.
Every request is attributed through tags minted into the key, so callers never send them per request.
Platform guarantees: tested fallbacks on every upgrade, scaling on in-flight requests instead of CPU, and provider alerts that reach tenants rather than being swallowed.
Upgrades flow dev, stage, prod via GitOps pull requests with a seven-day cooldown after a prod regression and API contract tests; CVE fixes skip the cooldown and ship the same day.

On Kubernetes: isolated namespaces with network policies, no keys in pods, tenant IAM roles, KEDA scaling on in-flight requests, PodDisruptionBudgets, long drain grace periods, Argo CD sync and rollback, and one Helm chart per region.
Next: multi-region with full in-region stacks for data residency, tenant-defined auto routing with evals to check cost/quality, and moving from keys to agent and workload identity.

numbers.text: Seven-day cooldown between dev and prod promotion for new LiteLLM versions.
The infrastructure team runs hundreds of clusters across clouds.

open_gaps.text: Data residency requires running the whole stack in one region, and not every provider offers every model in every region, so fallback config must also be region-bound. Still in design.
Keys still carry budgets and attribution; replacing them with agent identity tied to internal identity systems or Kubernetes service accounts is longer term.
Auto routing is only in pilot; tenants need a way to prove it gives the cost/quality tradeoff they want.

opportunities.text: Stamp an owning human or customer ID on every gateway key and enforce default budgets so agent-minted keys cannot bypass limits.
Autoscale LLM proxies on in-flight requests with KEDA instead of CPU.
Add API contract tests and a cooldown stage to your gateway upgrade pipeline, with a fast path for CVE fixes.
Describe a maturity model for your own AI gateway using the stages here: shared keys, team tenants, agents, platform guarantees.

title: Dropping LLM Inference Cost by Two-Thirds with Open Weights and Kubernetes
tldr: An AWS solutions architect replaced a proprietary LLM API in a multi-label classification pipeline with a QLoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3 8B model served by vLLM on EKS, raising exact-match accuracy from 56% to 91% at one-third of the cost. Quantization, prefix caching and speculative decoding raised per-GPU throughput, but surges exposed slow GPU capacity, which was fixed with smaller and pre-baked images and headroom.

key_points.text: Proprietary APIs cost scales one-to-one with traffic, you pay for intelligence a narrow task does not need, and model upgrades can break tuned prompts: one newer model broke the required JSON format.
The task is a single bounded call (pick every label that applies to a piece of feedback), so it needs a reliable specialist model, not an agent that plans.

Fine-tune when the task is narrow and repeats, you have labeled data, volume makes cost matter, prompting has plateaued and output must be predictable; stay on prompts when the task changes weekly, volume is low, reasoning is open-ended or there is no labeled data.
QLoRA with Unsloth trains a small adapter on a frozen 4-bit base; the adapter was then merged into the base, since there is only one task, instead of hot-swapping adapters with vLLM multi-LoRA.
Training recipe: JSON-formatted labeled data, rare multi-label records repeated three times to balance, rank 32 adapter, evaluation on a held-out unseen set.

The whole pipeline runs as Kubernetes Jobs on the serving cluster: CPU-only data prep, a GPU training job on a Karpenter pool capped as a spend guardrail, merge and AWQ quantization, and a vLLM eval that gates deployment on accuracy.
AWQ 4-bit quantization barely moved accuracy; the real payoff was freeing GPU memory for KV cache on a single A10G instance.
vLLM continuous batching, prefix caching and speculative decoding (answer IDs are copied from the prompt, so guesses are often right) added throughput without more GPUs.
Stack: EKS, Karpenter for GPU nodes, NVIDIA device plugin, one vLLM pod per GPU node, and Prometheus plus KEDA scaling on vLLM running and waiting requests; scale up fast, scale down slowly.
In a surge test the autoscaler asked for the right replicas but GPU capacity arrived late, so most requests timed out.
Fixes: zstd-compressed image on a fast disk, image and model pre-baked into the node image, headroom kept for bursts, and GPU capacity spread across regions.

numbers.text: One newer model broke the JSON output format 18% of the time.
Average prompt size grew from 1.5K to over 6K tokens in a year (OpenRouter study cited).
Exact-match accuracy: 56% for the best prompted general API, 12% for Qwen3 8B out of the box, 91% after fine-tuning.
About 10,000 labeled examples; adapter about 1% of the model (334 MB), trained on one GPU in about 12 hours.
Model shrank from 16 GB to 5.7 GB with 4-bit AWQ; KV cache capacity grew 3.6x from 27K tokens.
Serving on a G5 xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) at about $1 per hour on demand: 5.7 GB model, 12 GB KV cache.
42% more requests per GPU overall; P95 latency from 8.5 to 6.3; speculative decoding guesses accepted 62% of the time.
KEDA scales on in-flight requests divided by 16; Prometheus scrapes vLLM every 5 seconds; model load about 2 minutes.
Surge test: traffic rose 8x, queue climbed to 2,800 requests, KEDA asked for 10 replicas but got 1, and only 18% of requests were served.
Container image cut from 11 GB to 7.3 GB; image pull from 5 minutes to 1 minute; a new GPU node useful in about 4 minutes; 5% headroom kept.
Cost fell to 33% of the API baseline while accuracy rose from 56% to 91%.

open_gaps.text: Autoscalers react correctly but GPU capacity arrives too late for minute-scale surges.
GPU shortages mean capacity has to be spread across regions to get allocations quickly.
Platform automation (an account patch baseline) rebooted new GPU nodes minutes after launch, eating into burst capacity.
Fine-tuning does not fit tasks that change weekly, need open-ended reasoning or lack labeled data.

opportunities.text: Run fine-tune, quantize and eval-gated deploy as Kubernetes Jobs on the serving cluster, with a GPU-capped Karpenter pool for training.
Scale vLLM with KEDA on running plus waiting requests and pre-bake model images into GPU node images to cut cold start.
Measure how much GPU memory 4-bit AWQ frees for KV cache on your own model and instance type.
Publish a fine-tune-versus-prompt decision checklist with your own accuracy and cost numbers.

title: Quota Isn't Enough: Topology Aware Scheduling on Modern GPU Clusters
tldr: On NVL72 racks the NVLink domain is the whole rack, and leaving it drops bandwidth 18x, so having GPU quota no longer means a job will run fast or start at all. The speakers explain Kueue Topology Aware Scheduling and production lessons on test pods, slice sizing, node hot swap, preemption tickets, fragmentation and hero workloads.

key_points.text: A training collective runs at the speed of its slowest link; with NVL72, staying inside a rack keeps all traffic on NVLink, while the default scheduler and quota never ask where pods land.
Placing 9 GPUs on one rack and 7 on another makes every all-reduce round cross the network, though quota and scheduling look identical to Kubernetes.
Training wants powers of two, so jobs use 64 of each rack's 72 GPUs; without telling Kueue 64 is the unit, a 128-GPU job can land as 72 + 56.

TAS config: the platform declares a Topology (e.g. fabric, superpod, leaf group, NVLink domain, node) on a ResourceFlavor; users add one pod-template annotation; Kueue checks quota and shape at admission and pins pods with node selectors.

CoreWeave's idle-node verification pods blocked customer jobs once TAS counted them; fix was no Kueue queue label, the unconstrained topology annotation, and priority -1 so kube-scheduler preempts them.
Multi-rack jobs need a slice size (16 nodes of 4 GPUs = 64 GPUs per rack) for balanced placement; jagged allocations hurt speed and have triggered XLA crashes.
Annotation modes: unconstrained (inference, single-node), preferred (best effort, may land unbalanced, for post-training), required (wait for the right shape, for pre-training).

Node hot swap via the TAS failed-node-replacement feature gate replaces one pinned node within the same topology instead of re-queuing the whole job. Kueue only sees taints, set at CoreWeave by Node Problem Detector and verification tests.
Preemption tickets: Kueue preempts only if the pending job would fit after evictions, so quota math alone misleads users.
Fragmentation: job departures leave holes that do not align with racks; best-fit, least-capacity and balanced placement only slow the decay, since nothing moves running work.

Cohere fills spare rack nodes with preemptible inference via cohorts with quota borrowing, keeping hot spares for the largest jobs. For hero jobs, CoreWeave built a stop-gap rack-clearing controller; upstream Kueue now has configurable preemption that treats topology plus priority as a reason to preempt.

numbers.text: Bandwidths: memory 8 TB/s, NVLink 5 900 GB/s, host 450 GB/s, PCIe 64 GB/s, InfiniBand across racks 50 GB/s.
In-rack bandwidth is 18x faster than between racks on NVL72; on H100 the off-node drop was about 4.5x.
About $18,000 per day for one rack at published on-demand CoreWeave pricing.
NCCL all-reduce, 8 GB messages on four GB200 nodes: 908 GB/s bus bandwidth within a single rack.
Racks are delivered once 16 of 18 nodes are healthy; 64 of 72 GPUs are promised, 8 are failure allowance.
Hero workload example: 1,000 GPUs at highest priority.

open_gaps.text: Nothing in the system can defragment running work; admission policies only slow fragmentation.
Kueue only understands taints, so faults that pass every automated check (some NVLink degradation) put pods back on the same bad node repeatedly.
Kueue picks nodes and kube-scheduler places pods, so they can race; moving topology into kube-scheduler via workload-aware scheduling is future work.
Configurable preemption moves preemption to a global level, so who may defragment must be tightly controlled; wider defragmentation needs more work.

opportunities.text: Set required topology with slice sizes for pre-training jobs and preferred for post-training on rack-scale GPU clusters.
Wire GPU health signals (XID errors, NVLink faults, failed NCCL tests) into node taints so Kueue's failed-node replacement can act.
Work on Kueue defragmentation and moving topology awareness into kube-scheduler.
Build a dashboard that shows topology-aware free capacity per rack, not just quota, to answer 'why is my job pending'.

title: Agentic AI: Let’s Build a Reference Architecture, Live? Or at Least Try!
tldr: In a CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board session, Ricardo Rocha drew a layered agentic AI reference architecture live from audience input: gateway, orchestration, sandboxing, inference, infrastructure and observability. Attendees named their tools and gaps, mainly caller identity, data privacy and the lack of a shared agent harness, and were asked to submit their own reference architectures.

key_points.text: The End User TAB publishes end-user reference architectures at endusers.cncf.io: projects used, diagrams, what worked, what did not, and what glue had to be built.
Audience-proposed layers: gateway, data sources, inference, policies, network policies, and agent frameworks such as LangChain.
Identity: one attendee sees caller identity lost as requests move toward the model and wants it carried end to end, for example with SPIFFE/SPIRE or signing.
Another attendee, on AWS only, assumes a role through an IdP and SigV4-signs every request through the pipeline.
Privacy: one team tokenizes and anonymizes sensitive fields before they reach a model and reverses it on the response.
Gateway tools named: Envoy, agentgateway (split into MCP and LLM roles) and LiteLLM, used in front of Bedrock for routing, team access and quotas.
Egress control: per-agent allowlists of DNS names so each agent reaches only the domains its tools need.
One attendee embeds the harness in each web app to reuse the user's session and permissions, but gets no shared observability.
Some workloads are tens of thousands of one-shot agents that never resume, unlike long-running coding agents, which changes how useful pause and resume is.
Sandboxes named: Kata Containers, gVisor, Bubblewrap and Firecracker. Inference: NVIDIA Dynamo, Triton, vLLM, Ollama, SGLang and llama.cpp. Agent observability: Langfuse.
Multiple submissions in one area would let the TAB build a domain-level reference architecture from common patterns.

numbers.text: Show of hands: about five deploy only in public cloud, one only on premises, the rest mixed.
One use case has tens of thousands of agents with one to three turns each.
Example egress allowlist: about 10 domains per agent.

open_gaps.text: Caller identity is often lost between the agent layer and the inference engine, so requests cannot be attributed.
Privacy handling for data sent to third-party inference gets little attention at the conference.
No shared harness pattern: teams re-implement the harness per application, without common observability.
There is no stable reference architecture yet; teams are early and still iterating.

opportunities.text: Submit your agent platform as a CNCF end-user reference architecture, including what did not work and the glue you built.
Build a tokenization step that strips sensitive fields before inference and restores them in the response.
Enforce per-agent FQDN egress allowlists for agent workloads.
Join the End User TAB meetings or a domain user group to share agentic AI deployment feedback.

title: Demystifying Upgrades for Stateful, Dormant AI Agents: Unleashing Seamless Updates in Dynamic Sandboxes
tldr: Cloud-hosted agent sandboxes need near-daily harness and CVE updates, but their state (sessions, skills, installed tools) sits in the container's writable layer and is lost on restart. OpenKruise Agents offers upgrade paths for warm pools, sandbox claims, and running or paused sandboxes, plus a session-aware sandbox service for fleet-level rollouts.

key_points.text: Agent harnesses need frequent, often daily, updates for features and CVE patches, while sandbox state such as session context, skills and installed tools is lost when the sandbox restarts.
Sandboxes lack Deployment- or StatefulSet-style workload support, so phased rollout and replica control are left to operators.
Lifecycle: ready in a warm pool, running once claimed with a session, then idle and usually paused to save compute.
OpenKruise Agents uses pods as sandboxes and exposes an E2B API for AI engineers and a Kubernetes API for infra teams; storage can be static mounts or on-demand mounts set at claim time.
Warm pool refresh is easy: the sandbox set behaves like a Deployment, with max-unavailable and max-surge controls.
At claim time the image can be swapped (e.g. to a canary) and resources raised through in-place pod resizing, so a small warm pool can serve larger requests.
Idle detection is time-based or probe-based: a node daemon repeatedly runs a command in the sandbox asking the agent whether it has active sessions.
A sandbox update job selects sandboxes by label and state; paused sandboxes are woken, upgraded and paused again.
Core problem: you cannot freely change the image (lower layer) while keeping the overlay writable layer; mixing them gives an unpredictable file system.

Strategies for running sandboxes: recreate with pre/post-upgrade backup hooks, in-place update (e.g. sidecars, or emptyDir as backup), checkpoint-restore for non-image changes, and an installer upgrade that injects an ephemeral container to copy in new files.
Sandbox service gives a stable endpoint; a gateway maps session IDs to sandboxes and drains old sandboxes during a rollout.

numbers.text: In production about 99% of sandboxes are hibernated; only 1 in 100 is running.

open_gaps.text: Recreate upgrades require knowing which data to save and having shared storage, and LLMs may install files outside the directory you told them to use.
Agent applications have poor backward compatibility between versions, so upgrades can break; checkpoint-then-rollback is planned for risky upgrades.
The installer upgrade strategy is not released yet; it is planned for the next release.

opportunities.text: Take a file-system-only checkpoint before each agent sandbox upgrade and roll back to it if the upgrade fails.
Add an idle probe to your agent harness that reports active sessions, so upgrades only touch idle sandboxes.
How the overlay file system splits image layers from the writable layer, and why that blocks naive in-place image upgrades.
