Try the sandbox upgrade strategies in OpenKruise Agents and report agent-specific state that hooks fail to capture.

title: Fireside Chat: Future of Kubernetes and Agents with Tim Hockin and Kelsey Hightower
tldr: Savannah Peterson hosts Tim Hockin and Kelsey Hightower on why agents need a different platform layer: they are untrusted, mostly idle and single-tenant, which normal Kubernetes patterns serve with poor startup times or poor utilization. They frame Agent Substrate as Kubernetes extended for a new workload, urge teams to check they need an agent at all, and name delegated identity and permission scoping as open problems.

key_points.text: Hightower: an agent differs from a shell script in taking unstructured input and making its own decisions; the work is limiting it to only the problem you asked it to solve.
Hockin: agents are untrusted ("malware in a box") so must be sandboxed, spend most of their life asleep waiting for input, and are single-tenant.
Together these give either poor user experience from repeated startups or single-digit cluster CPU utilization; Agent Substrate aims to fix both on Kubernetes.
Hightower: new workloads reshape the platform, as microservices forced observability; Knative and Istio are earlier examples of building a workload platform on Kubernetes.
A 2 to 4 second container start is fine for services that run for weeks, but not for an agent that works 500 ms and sleeps again.
Hightower: most of Agent Substrate's technology already existed; it is packaged for this workload.
Security defaults: sandboxing cannot be turned off, agents have no network without permission, egress goes to a pluggable policy enforcement point, and every agent has its own identity.
Advice: start small and try it on something unimportant (Hockin); first confirm the task needs an agent, recalling how serverless functions grew into VMs (Hightower).
Per-team clusters or central control: teams that already run clusters can try it; otherwise use a dedicated node pool or dedicated cluster, partly because Substrate needs a recent Kubernetes version.
On-behalf-of identity: v1 has its own identity and issuer; down-scoped user identity (OBO) is being discussed with users and is not done.
For an SRE agent, give it only the tools, data sources and network paths the on-call human uses, and constrain it with skill files.

numbers.text: Container start of 2 to 4 seconds versus an agent run of about 500 ms.
People have used agents in earnest for about a year and a half.
Audience show of hands: roughly 50/50 between actively building with AI and wanting to start.

open_gaps.text: Carrying a user's identity through agents with down-scoped on-behalf-of tokens is not done yet in Agent Substrate.
Open-ended agents push teams to grant broad permissions up front; scoping permissions for tasks you cannot predict is unsolved.
v1 will not fit everyone: users are asking for bring-your-own identity and new network and other policies.

opportunities.text: Try Agent Substrate on a non-critical workload in a test cluster, ideally on a dedicated node pool.
Scope an SRE agent's sandbox to the exact tools and network paths an on-call engineer needs, and nothing else.
Give the project feedback on identity needs such as on-behalf-of flows and bring-your-own identity.
Map which of your automation tasks need an agent and which should stay fixed-behavior scripts.

title: Frameworkless ML Serving: Scaling to Thousands of Models with KEDA, Pub/Sub, and Native K8s
tldr: Isomorphic Labs moved from Vertex AI to Ray Serve to a framework-free platform where every model is a stateless Kubernetes Deployment pulling from its own Pub/Sub queue behind a stateless gateway. KEDA scales workers to zero, Kubernetes priority and preemption put interactive traffic ahead of batch, and narrow interfaces let them swap storage backends live.

key_points.text: Workloads are framework-agnostic Python inference graphs on GKE; thousands of models share one compute pool, and each prediction holds an accelerator for minutes, not milliseconds.

Vertex AI kept at least one replica per model, so idle cost grew with the catalog. Ray Serve on Kubernetes added a second scheduler, a head node per graph, image rebuilds for resource tweaks, and in-memory requests that scale on concurrency.

Their requirements (any accelerator, no duplicate predictions, scale to zero, interactive preempting batch) mostly described Kubernetes itself, so they built on a stateless worker plus an asynchronous queue.

Request flow: the gateway checks a GCS result store by a hash of input and worker, then a Bigtable status store for pending work, publishes to the worker's Pub/Sub topic, and returns 'pending'. Clients poll with the same request.
Workers pull from their subscription, keep the lease alive while computing, send output to the gateway, and ack after the gateway stores it.

DAGs use 're-enter and check and sleep': a parent that gets 'pending' from a child acks and exits; when the child finishes, the gateway republishes the parent request, which reruns deterministically and now hits the cached result.
A KEDA ScaledObject per worker watches its Pub/Sub backlog, wakes the Deployment from zero to one, and hands off to HPA, which scales by requests per pod.
Each worker priority maps to a Kubernetes PriorityClass; preempting a low-priority pod is safe because its Pub/Sub lease expires and the message is redelivered.
A small Python SDK hides Pub/Sub, leases, serialization and child calls: researchers subclass a worker and implement handle_message.

Lessons: start simple, choose high-ceiling primitives, and put every backend behind a narrow interface (factory/strategy pattern) so it can be swapped. A Redis cache in front of GCS evicted keys and caused recomputation; removing it made two of four hot paths slightly faster.
GitOps acts as the model store: a PR with a short YAML file is compiled by Kapitan into manifests that Argo CD syncs; retiring a model means removing it from Git.

numbers.text: Preemption example: 200 accelerators, two low-priority workers each scaled to 100 pods.
Gateway scales to thousands of stateless replicas; workers scale from zero to thousands of pods.
Hashing Redis keys cut per-key memory in half, doubling the in-flight limit.
Interfaces built in week one still allowed live database swaps three and a half years later.
Ray-based setup was outgrown about six months in.

open_gaps.text: Every model leaves a footprint (subscriptions, ScaledObjects, Deployments); at thousands of models this hits per-project Pub/Sub caps, handled by garbage collection and sharding queues across GCP projects.
Managed Redis for in-flight status hit its top size tier and connection limit, forcing per-pod connection rationing until a dual-write migration to Bigtable.
A dedicated model registry will be needed at some point; Git is a stopgap.

opportunities.text: Serve long-running models as queue-backed stateless workers with KEDA scale-to-zero and PriorityClass-based preemption.
Put durable result and status stores behind narrow interfaces with in-memory fakes so you can dual-write and flip backends with a config flag.
Compare this queue-and-poll design with framework serving (Ray Serve, KServe) for minute-long predictions.
The 're-enter and check and sleep' pattern for running DAGs without blocking accelerators.

title: From GPU to Fleet. The llm-d KV Cache Hierarchy
tldr: Agent traffic is long input and short output, so reusing KV cache matters more than raw GPU speed. llm-d and vLLM now tier KV cache from GPU to CPU to shared storage and route requests to where the cache already lives.

key_points.text: Agentic workloads read far more than they write; KV cache reuse can reach 95%.
Tiering is upstream: vLLM ships an offloading connector (GPU to CPU to storage, CPU as the core tier) and a storage connector; llm-d owns orchestration and eviction.
Peer-to-peer KV transfer pulls a prefix from a busy pod to a free one, and also powers prefill/decode disaggregation.
Three tiers: GPU HBM (hottest, smallest), CPU DRAM plus local NVMe (about 2 TB), and shared network storage such as Lustre or IBM Storage Scale.
Plain NFS volumes do not scale for this; parallel file systems give the throughput needed.
Storage offloading without storage-aware routing fails at scale: requests land on pods that do not hold the cache.
Setup: an RWX PVC, pinned CPU memory and the offloading connector on vLLM (SGLang also supported), plus KV events and endpoint-picker config in the llm-d router.

numbers.text: An 80 GB GPU leaves about 15 GB for KV cache after model weights and buffers.
Over 50% TCO savings and about 60% fewer GPU hours with external storage attached.
About 40% better time to first token and 30% more QPS with the hybrid setup.
Llama 70B at 128k tokens: reading KV from network storage is about 10x faster than recomputing.
Speedup over recompute: HBM about 40x, DRAM about 21x, network storage about 10x.
Replayed Claude Code traces, 50 to 800 users: GPU-only saturates past 100 users; GPU+CPU hits a cliff near 300; GPU+CPU+storage stays flat above 2,500 output tok/s up to 800 users.
Turning off the storage index in the router dropped throughput from about 2,500 to 700 tok/s at 800 users.
About 1.2 billion KV tokens written to storage in the run.

open_gaps.text: Writing a new KV connector in vLLM used to be very hard; the new offloading connector is meant to make it pluggable, and more connectors are wanted.
KV footprint keeps growing with context length (up to a million tokens), so capacity planning across tiers is an ongoing problem.
The speakers ask for more contributions to the guides and to the KV Cache SIG.

opportunities.text: Reproduce the GPU-only vs GPU+CPU vs GPU+CPU+storage curve on a managed Kubernetes service with a shared file system (for example FSx for Lustre) and publish the guide.
Add a storage backend to the vLLM offloading connector or an llm-d well-lit-path guide for another cloud's parallel file system.
Explain 'storage offloading needs storage-aware routing' with the 2,500 vs 700 tok/s result as the hook.
Join the llm-d KV Cache SIG to follow tiering and P2P work.

title: Running Secure Agents at Scale
tldr: Adobe Experience Manager runs a few thousand single-tenant agents that import and redesign customer websites, each needing a sandboxed Playwright browser. After comparing Agent Sandbox, OpenShell, Substrate and others, Adobe chose Agent Sandbox with warm pools because its agents run long sessions rather than short bursts.

key_points.text: Customers chat with an agent that imports a site into the platform and edits its design, with a live preview; Adobe needs to run a few thousand of these agents.

Design: one user per pod, because agents hold state and can write and run code; persistent storage for generated files; no credentials stored in the agent, since agents can be tricked into exfiltrating them.
Pain points: read-write-once volumes cause downtime when a user's pod is replaced, large images (browsers, Playwright) slow cold starts, and idle agents waste resources.

Playwright runs in its own sandbox, separate from the agent: Chromium is stateful and cannot be shared across users, and splitting lifecycles keeps the agent from paying the browser's startup cost when a chat does not need it.

Options compared in a public repo: Agent Sandbox (warm pools, gVisor or Kata), OpenShell (built on Agent Sandbox, adds a supervisor for policy, DNS and credential injection), Substrate (own scheduler, suspend and resume with snapshots), and smaller projects.

A Playwright proxy maps each caller to a browser sandbox by looking up the calling pod's labels from its source IP; labels are trusted because agents have no Kubernetes API access, while request contents could be faked.

Agent Sandbox resources: SandboxTemplate (pod spec), warm pool (replica count per template), SandboxClaim (takes a sandbox from the pool) and Sandbox, all managed by its controller. Deleting the claim gives a fresh browser.
Substrate was not chosen: it was early and has many moving parts, and its suspend/resume fits bursty, mostly idle agents, while Adobe's agents run for hours.

Selection guide: Agent Sandbox for fast assignment and simplicity, OpenShell for more policy and services around the agent, Substrate for bursty short-lived workloads; the speaker notes cloud providers appear to be converging on Substrate.
Production setup keeps a warm pool of three Playwright sandboxes; clients needed no code change, only a remote Playwright endpoint. Readiness means waiting until Chromium's ports are open.
Q&A: agent pods are Claude Code clients that call the LLM and use Playwright as a tool; the sandbox runtime is gVisor, which the speaker sees as the most supported.

numbers.text: A few thousand agents to run.
Warm pool of three Playwright sandbox replicas kept running.

open_gaps.text: Most volumes can only be mounted for writing by one pod, so replacing a user's pod causes downtime.
Not everything Playwright offers is exposed through MCP yet, so Adobe also exposes WebSockets.
Warm pools cost resources while idle sandboxes wait, and the sandboxing landscape is changing week to week.

opportunities.text: Study the speaker's public repo that runs Playwright on each sandbox implementation and compares them.
Put heavy tools like browsers in their own warm-pooled sandboxes behind a proxy that assigns them by pod identity, not by request contents.
Benchmark sandbox startup time and resource cost for long-running versus bursty agent workloads across Agent Sandbox, OpenShell and Substrate.
Give feedback to Agent Sandbox on lifecycle and readiness handling for stateful tools like Chromium.

title: Choose Your Own Adventure: The Saga of Serving LLM Inference
tldr: The audience voted on three vLLM serving choices (quantization, sharding versus replication, speculative decoding) and the speakers deployed that configuration and its opposite side by side under load. The audience's full-precision, sharded, speculative setup was more accurate but served fewer requests, and the speakers' advice is to run experiments, not pick in advance.

key_points.text: The audience chose full precision, one model sharded across two GPUs, and n-gram speculative decoding; a second deployment used the opposite choices.
A model scores every possible next token (about 150,000 for the demo model) and the inference engine picks one; knowledge is spread across all weights, so almost all weights are read for every token.

Weights and KV cache compete for GPU memory; quantization stores each weight with fewer bits, freeing room for more and longer conversations and reducing memory reads, at the cost of drifting from how the model was trained.
Switching to the quantized variant was just a different model image (Qwen3 8B to its FP8 version); not every model can go to 4 bits.
Replication gives independent engines, KV caches and no GPU-to-GPU traffic but needs a model small enough and sticky routing; sharding splits weights and KV cache and needs fast GPU interconnect.
Replication tends to win with many concurrent requests and enough KV cache; sharding tends to win with few requests, fast links, or models too big for one GPU.
Sharding was configured as one copy on two GPUs plus tensor parallel size 2 passed to vLLM.
Prefill processes known tokens in parallel and is compute-bound; decode is sequential and memory-bandwidth-bound.

Speculative decoding drafts several tokens (here n-gram, deterministic pattern matching on the conversation) and the model verifies them in one pass, trading compute for memory bandwidth; it is less useful when the GPU is already at high load.
Advice: you cannot make these choices in advance; serve variants in parallel with round-robin routing and compare. The demo sent telemetry via OpenTelemetry to Datadog.

numbers.text: Demo model: Qwen3 8B, 8 billion parameters, 16-bit weights by default.
Each demo GPU has 24 GB of memory; at full precision about 3 GB per GPU is left for conversations.
Quantized, about 9 GB would hold weights and 9.6 GB would be free for conversations.
The audience's configuration served 30-40% fewer requests and processed fewer tokens per second.
The audience's full-precision configuration answered the math test prompts 100% correctly.
Speculative decoding drafted up to four tokens ahead.

open_gaps.text: Whether quantization hurts answers for your use case has to be measured with your own experiments.
Many requests failed on the audience's configuration for reasons the speakers did not have time to explore.
Some models have no prebuilt quantized image, which makes quantizing painful.

opportunities.text: Deploy two vLLM configurations side by side with round-robin routing and compare throughput and accuracy on your own prompts.
Prefill versus decode bottlenecks (compute versus memory bandwidth) and how speculative decoding trades one for the other.
Add a small accuracy check (for example known math prompts) to load tests when evaluating quantized models.
Benchmark replication versus tensor-parallel sharding on your GPU interconnect at different concurrency levels.

title: Pods Are Not Enough for AI Agents, Meet Agent-substrate
tldr: Christian Posta argues that agents break microservice assumptions: they run unknown code, hold state and sit idle, so a session per pod overloads Kubernetes. Agent Substrate decouples actors from worker pods, snapshots idle actors to storage, wakes them on request, and forces all egress through policy with credential injection; kagent supplies the agent-aware layer on top.

key_points.text: Microservice assumptions (known code, stateless replicas, many users per pod, pods running hot) do not hold for agents, which write and run untested code, accumulate state and wait for humans or events.
Running one sandboxed pod per session, plus short-lived tool sandboxes, creates far more objects than the Kubernetes API server is built for.
Agent Substrate decouples a session (actor) from compute; actor state lives in Substrate's own control plane, not in Kubernetes custom resources.
Kubernetes still runs the compute: a WorkerPool custom resource defines worker pods, volumes and sandbox class, while actor templates and actors are Substrate objects.
Idle actors are snapshotted out of workers and rehydrated on any worker; identity is durable across the actor's life, and a request to a paused actor triggers activation through the router.
Snapshot level is configurable: root FS only, root FS plus workspace (durable directory), or those plus memory. Snapshots go to pluggable S3-compatible or GCS storage, with state in Postgres.
Demo: three actors from one template; two fill a single worker, one is suspended to make room, and scaling workers from one to two lets a router call wake the third.
Actors run in gVisor or microVM sandboxes and are treated as hostile: DNS, UDP and TCP egress is blocked unless a policy allows it.
Credential brokering: the actor sends a placeholder and agentgateway on the egress path injects the real token from OpenBao, so the agent never holds the secret.
Pod workload identity cannot tell apart actors sharing a pod; an identity policy adds a per-actor JWT so the destination can attribute the call.
Substrate knows nothing about agents, MCP or conversations; kagent (1.0 this week) decides when to snapshot and handles agent revisions and rollouts.

numbers.text: Control plane target: hundreds of millions, up to a billion object changes per cluster.
North Star: a billion actors per cluster and activation in 100 ms or less.
Solo.io and Google started collaborating on Agent Substrate around April or May.

open_gaps.text: Substrate can snapshot on command, but knowing when to pause an actor needs an agent-aware layer above it.
Without an actor identity policy, the destination only sees a shared bot token and cannot attribute calls to an actor.
Harnesses keep leaking bearer credentials placed inside agents, which pushes teams to broker credentials outside the sandbox.

opportunities.text: Broker agent credentials on the egress path (placeholder in, real token injected from a vault) instead of putting API keys in the sandbox.
Write a Substrate storage or credential-provider plugin; storage is pluggable outside the main tree.
Use the Substrate calculator on kagent.dev to compare actor density and idle-pod cost for your workloads.
Read the agentgateway blog series on credential brokering and blast radius.

title: Cache Me If You Can: LLM Inference with llm-d (with fun drawings)
tldr: A step-by-step tour of llm-d: how the endpoint picker filters, scores and picks a pod, and where prefix-aware routing, KV offloading and prefill/decode disaggregation fit. Most of the talk is a practical guide to flow control: saturation detectors, fairness policies and priority holdback.

key_points.text: Once one model server fills up, adding replicas needs smarter routing than round robin, or you keep recomputing cache.
The gateway asks llm-d's endpoint picker (EPP) which pod in an InferencePool to use; the key resources are the EPP, InferenceObjective, InferencePool, Gateway and HTTPRoute.
The EPP filters, scores, then picks. It estimates which prefixes each pod holds from the requests it sent; it does not read pod caches.
Prefix affinity can pile traffic onto one hot pod; adding a load score trades cache hits against queue time.
KV offload to CPU keeps long agentic sessions reusable; prefill/decode disaggregation separates bursty prefill from steady decode.
Batch inference runs through an OpenAI-compatible batch gateway and an async processor that dispatches when there is room.
Flow control: priority bands hold per-tenant queues, and it only gates when the pool is saturated. Fairness policies include global strict (oldest first), round robin, and least-served first.
Saturation detectors can count requests or tokens, read engine utilization (which lags), or combine both; gate too early and you lose throughput, too late and GPUs oversaturate.
Priority holdback stops batch from being admitted above a pool saturation threshold, so real-time latency stays as if batch were not there.
Other levers: SLO-based ordering, headroom, quota-based priority, and evicting batch work back to the queue for retry.
Tune by symptom, one knob at a time, and check llm-d's prefix guesses against vLLM's own metrics.

numbers.text: Priority holdback example: batch held back when total pool saturation is above 0.6, tested on H100.

open_gaps.text: Output-token estimation is off by default and needs extra infrastructure; request-count detectors break down when request sizes vary widely.
Utilization-based detection lags and can over-admit.
There are many knobs and little tooling to see their effect; the speaker built a replay visualizer and interactive explainer and hopes to contribute them.

opportunities.text: Mix batch and real-time traffic on one pool, turn on priority holdback, and measure real-time P95.
Help bring the interactive explainer or run-replay visualizer into the llm-d docs.
A guide to choosing a saturation detector for a given traffic shape.
Use this talk as a walkthrough while deploying llm-d's well-lit paths.

title: Zero-Gap GPU Execution: Building Secure, Pre-Warmed Pod Runtimes for High-Velocity AI Agents
tldr: LinkedIn built Firepool, a broker that keeps warm GPU pods ready so agents and RL loops running on CPU nodes can launch GPU jobs without Kubernetes pod startup in the critical path. Its zero-gap mode uses HAMi and Volcano to park standby pods on a busy GPU so the next job takes over the card the moment the current one ends.

key_points.text: Motivating workloads: Autopilot (an agent migrating TensorFlow models to PyTorch for tens of hours), an auto-research agent running experiments for days, and agentic RL rollouts. All need GPUs repeatedly but not continuously.
Running agents on GPU nodes wastes GPUs while they think; running them on CPU nodes and launching a GPU pod per step pays a cold start every iteration.

The Firepool broker has a REST API, job store and pool controller for capacity, plus a dispatcher, in-memory pod tracker and executors; each pod runs a lightweight Firepool agent that fetches and runs the job code.

The API is built for agents: submit returns a job ID immediately, unknown fields are rejected to block hallucinated input, retries stay under one job ID, and failures return a specific error class and exit code.

Pod selection order: the caller's own idle pod, then a never-used idle pod, then a standby on a busy GPU, and only last a new pod. Claiming happens in one step under one lock; multi-pod jobs claim all pods at once, gang-style.
Pods start with a shared base image (CUDA, framework); user code, extra Python packages and distributed rank/addresses arrive with the job, so one pool serves many environments.
Safe reuse rules: verified reset of the process tree, code and shared memory (else delete the pod), owner-only reuse, and a reuse tag that marks a pod for retirement when a different tag lands on it.

Pools are sized from the job queue, not GPU utilization, with four knobs: floor, ceiling, idle wait time, and idle pods kept after that. Firepool can borrow idle GPUs from other teams and return them on demand.
Zero gap uses HAMi only for scheduling multiple pods per GPU (no partitioning or time sharing); one pod runs a job with the full card while standby pods wait to be promoted.

Sandboxing: pods have no egress by default; all outbound traffic goes through a sidecar proxy that holds the credentials, injects them and checks policy. A checkpoint daemon persists agent state, and shared memory lets agent instances share learnings.
Q&A: Firepool only uses spare capacity and does not run production training; fragmentation is handled with fixed GPU SKU types and custom Volcano bin-packing plugins.

numbers.text: New GPU pod cold start with cached image: 20-30 seconds; uncached image: 2-10 minutes.
Binding a job to a warm pod takes under half a second.
Median handover time with a different reuse tag per job dropped from 51 seconds to under a second.
A new GPU pod takes about 22 seconds to run its first instruction; on a warm pod job code starts in about a second.
In an H200 benchmark, an agent loop went from 26 minutes to 2.
19 of 20 pod requests in production are served from warm pods (standbys included).
Auto-research agent runs have lasted 7 days.
Autopilot cut TensorFlow-to-PyTorch migration time per model from months to about a week.

open_gaps.text: Standby pods with different container images on the same GPU are not supported yet; it is the next step, aimed at many RL environments on a small GPU budget.
When the cluster is full, plain warm pools cannot grow and jobs wait for capacity again; agents now mostly wait on quota rather than cold start.
Pod reuse is not a security boundary: state outside tracked writable paths is handled by read-only pods and opt-out, not full isolation.
Firepool is not open source yet; the team plans to release it.

opportunities.text: Add a warm-pod broker in front of GPU jobs for agent loops, sized from queue depth with floor and ceiling knobs.
Use HAMi scheduling slots with Volcano to park standby pods on busy GPUs and cut handover gaps between tenants.
Follow Firepool's planned open-source release and help with multi-image standby support.
Sidecar credential injection with no-egress pods as a pattern for running untrusted agent code.

title: Many Clusters, One GPU Pool: Locality-Aware Scheduling and Data Delivery With Kueue and Dragonfly
tldr: Roblox joined five Kubernetes clusters across three AWS regions and its own data center into one GPU pool with MultiKueue, a custom external dispatcher and tiered quotas. Dragonfly P2P caching in each cluster turned repeated cross-region S3 reads into local and peer reads for training data and model weights.

key_points.text: Before: one cluster in us-east-1 with a YuniKorn-based scheduler; GPUs sat idle while reserved, jobs were interrupted often, and upgrades hit every training job at once.
GPU capacity appeared in different regions with short windows to grab it, while training data stayed in S3 in us-east-1.
They compared YuniKorn, Karmada and MultiKueue; Kueue already had tiers, borrowing and preemption, and MultiKueue extends them across clusters with an external dispatcher hook.
Design principles: stay upstream, isolate cluster failures, users never pick a cluster, fail open if custom parts break, cloud-agnostic job specs.

A hub cluster holds global quota and is the only submission point; jobs set GPU type, priority tier and data region labels, and each spoke's local Kueue checks real node capacity. The first spoke to admit runs the job.
The external dispatcher ranks spokes: hard checks first (framework, GPU type, EFA/RDMA, volumes, full gang fit), then a time-limited preference for the data's region.
Three tiers: guaranteed (owned quota), shared (borrowing idle GPUs) and opportunistic (spot); spokes put guaranteed and shared queues in one cohort so owners can reclaim borrowed GPUs.
On-prem differences (own SKUs, SR-IOV RDMA, separate RDMA stripes, fixed racks) stay in spoke ResourceFlavors, so job specs remain cloud agnostic.
Dragonfly caches S3 objects per cluster: each piece is read from the node's cache, a peer, a seed peer, then S3; if Dragonfly components fail, clients fall back to S3.

A data mobility controller called Fairy pre-stages weights and checkpoints and moves volumes across AZs and regions with the CSI snapshot controller and Velero; they are experimenting with CRIU snapshots for faster LLM inference startup.
Q&A: cache keys are S3 URLs on dedicated NVMe; LIST and GET authorization always goes to S3, so pods without IAM access cannot read cached data.

numbers.text: Five clusters across three AWS regions plus one on-prem data center; the hub serves about 500 team namespaces.
Each spoke reports free GPU capacity to the hub every 30 seconds.
The gang-fit check blocks about 5,000 partial fits a day.
Data-region preference lasts 5 minutes; almost 9 in 10 jobs still run in their data region.
80% more useful training work per reserved GPU hour, and 80% fewer job interruptions, versus the old single cluster.
93% of bytes read were repeat reads; about 15 TB of hot data caused about 3.5 PB of repeat downloads; the top 10 datasets were half of all transfers.
Dragonfly delivered over 9 PB since April: 50% from local cache, 43% from peers, 7% from S3.
Model weight loads about 9x faster; a GLM 5 series model took about 23 minutes from S3 and under 3 minutes once cached.
Over half of workloads now run outside us-east-1.
Cache TTL is one week on GPU nodes and two weeks on CPU peer nodes.

open_gaps.text: MultiKueue requires identical hub and spoke specs, which breaks with mutating webhooks; they want matching on quota fields only.
Preemption happens per spoke with no global view, and RayJobs are not validated on the hub, so invalid jobs can hold quota.
No support for dynamic quota when capacity blocks expire every few weeks.
Dragonfly caching stays off spot nodes, still needs RDMA support, and lacks a declarative Kubernetes-style API.

opportunities.text: Use the MultiKueue external dispatcher API to add data-locality and capacity-aware spoke ranking with a fallback timeout.
Put Dragonfly in front of S3 for training data and model weights after checking access logs for repeat reads.
Help MultiKueue with spec matching under mutating webhooks, global preemption and dynamic quota.
Add a declarative API and RDMA support to Dragonfly.

title: New Traffic, New Rules: Standardizing AI-Aware Networking in Kubernetes
tldr: The Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group presents its proposals for AI-aware traffic in Gateway API: pre-routing payload processing, a Backend resource, an endpoint selector, gateway routability and multi-stage routes. The goal is one standard set of APIs so different routers stop building their own body parsing, egress and inference orchestration.

key_points.text: The working group started about a year ago to standardize AI-aware traffic management at the gateway layer, reusing Gateway API building blocks and adding primitives only where they are missing.
Gateway API routes on headers, path and query, but AI signals such as the model name live in the request body. Today everyone solves this with ext_proc, Lua or Wasm, none of it standard.

Pre-routing filters, already in experimental, run an ordered list of filters before route selection. Paired with a filter that promotes a body field to a header, this enables body-based routing in process; external processing is future work.

Service does two jobs: a producer-owned front end (stable DNS name, cluster IP) and a consumer-oriented back end (endpoints, ports, protocol). Service is effectively frozen, so new features are hard to add there.

AI apps call external model APIs constantly, and ExternalName services are seen as unsafe and often banned. The new Backend resource, now experimental in Gateway API, covers in-cluster endpoint selectors or external hostnames plus TLS and protocol settings.
Backend does not replace Service; it is a fit-for-purpose place to add things like session persistence, TLS and later MCP.

Inference routers such as the llm-d endpoint picker need a bag of endpoints without a cluster IP, because clients using the Service VIP or DNS name bypass the picker and lose KV cache hits. The endpoint selector proposal to upstream Kubernetes reuses label-selector machinery for this.

The routability proposal lets a Gateway declare how its address is reachable (for example cluster-only), which matters for egress gateways that would otherwise become open relays. It is not access control; that remains NetworkPolicy.

Distributed inference no longer maps one request to one endpoint: a request may pass tokenization, guardrails, then encode, prefill and decode. Multi-stage routes reference existing HTTPRoutes and control stage order and skip conditions, reusing their retries and backoff.
Payload processing defines what happens between stages, such as passing prefill output as metadata to the decode request; the scheduling intelligence stays in the application layer.
Q&A: keep using Service for normal workloads; Backend is for specialized cases, AI or complex mesh setups, where endpoints need extra metadata.

open_gaps.text: External processing for payload handling is not yet supported; only in-process filters are in scope so far.
Multi-stage route syntax is illustrative and not finalized, and the between-stage data passing still has to be defined.
Next proposals include token-based rate limiting, plus consolidating the separate AI networking efforts in SIG Network into one community.
Routability cannot control what the cloud provider network exposes, so cluster scope is not a security guarantee.

opportunities.text: Join the AI Gateway Working Group calls and help move payload processing, Backend and multi-stage routes toward GA.
Prototype body-based model routing using pre-routing filters that promote the model field to a header.
Read the Kubernetes blog post on the Backend resource and compare it to how your gateway handles external model egress and TLS today.
Map how existing distributed inference projects orchestrate tokenize, prefill and decode stages, as input to the multi-stage route design.

title: Agents Fail. Workflows Recover. Durable Agent Orchestration with Cadence
tldr: Uber's Cadence team shows how wrapping model and tool calls as Cadence activities lets an agent resume after rate limits or worker crashes instead of starting over. Uber's Agent Executor Service already runs hundreds of thousands of agentic workflows on Cadence, and its execution history pointed straight at the cause of most timeouts.

key_points.text: Each model or tool call is a Cadence activity, a workflow orders them, and a worker runs the code; Cadence records progress in a separate service so a replacement worker can reuse completed results.
Workflows can wait for external input, such as a human decision, or for time to pass.
Smarter models do not prevent disks failing, APIs going down or workers crashing, so systems must assume every component fails.
Common agent failures: rate limits, endless loops, overconfident unsupported conclusions, stalls waiting on human review, and worker process crashes.
Cadence stores only the inputs and outputs of each step; it knows where the workflow is, not the business logic.
Demo: an on-call agent analyzing a checkout 500 error gets rate limited fetching logs, and Cadence retries automatically with configurable retryable and non-retryable error types.
A human sends a guidance signal to the workflow when the first answer has low confidence; the agent replans and traces the error to an exhausted ledger connection pool.
When the worker is killed, a new worker replays the stored history to rebuild state, with no repeated tool calls, and then takes the approval signal.
Workflow reset works as an undo for agents: roll back to a step before a bad decision instead of asking the agent to repair it.
Timeout breakdowns from Cadence observability narrowed the problem to one under-provisioned worker pool.

Q&A: Temporal forked from Cadence; Cadence works with agent sandboxes per activity and sits at the application layer above deployment substrates; avoid hot shards and use continue-as-new for long histories.

numbers.text: Cadence serves over 4,000 use cases at Uber.
The Agent Executor Service, built in July, hosted around 830,000 agentic workflows on Cadence by September.
Service error analyzer: 36,000 runs in 30 days, about 6,000 of them timed out.
In a newer measurement, zero runs of that agent timed out, failed or were terminated.
In the failure-injected demo, Cadence halved model responses and input, output and total tokens, with zero new calls during recovery.
About two-thirds of runs completed, a third timed out, and very few failed.
Over 32,000 runs completed despite at least one earlier failure.
50% of timeouts came from missing worker responses, another third from activity pickup, and over 99% occurred in one worker pool.
Temporal forked from Cadence in 2019.

open_gaps.text: Built-in guardrail functions are not yet part of the current agent framework integrations.
Cadence cannot fix workflow logic errors that teams write themselves; those still surface as timeouts.
More agent framework integrations are needed beyond Google ADK and OpenAI Agents; the team asks for contributions.
Workflow history size is limited, so long-running agents need continue-as-new.

opportunities.text: Run the live demo from the Cadence AI samples repo, including the injected failures.
Add a Cadence integration for another agent framework, or guardrail activities for existing ones.
Wrap each model and tool call in an agent as a durable activity with explicit retry policies and a human approval signal.
Break down agent timeouts by cause (worker response, activity pickup, heartbeat) to find under-provisioned worker pools.

title: Agents on the Platform: Four Perspectives on the Conversation We're Already Having in Private
tldr: A panel with platform, OpenTelemetry, security and inference perspectives discusses what platform teams must provide to run agents: sandboxing, identity, observability and inference routing. The shared advice is to rely on maturing community projects, treat agents as adversarial, instrument them from within, and learn the stack hands-on before rushing.

key_points.text: Sandbox runtimes are now commodity; build your own only for differentiated needs such as regulated environments or special file system access.
Agent lifecycle raises new ownership questions, such as which identity an agent takes when it resumes after suspension.
Security view: agent workloads should be considered adversarial, and standard containers are not an isolation boundary; use micro VMs without a shared kernel.
For inference, agents are long-running and bursty, so routing must reach the GPU that holds the cached context to avoid paying for uncached tokens.
HTTP 200 does not mean an agent did its job; compare routing guesses (e.g. llm-d prefix routing) with what actually happened, across multiple turns.
External observation is not enough for agents; they need instrumentation from within, like business instrumentation in microservices.
Many agent frameworks now conform to OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, but these are not yet stable because the underlying protocols keep changing.
Tracing has become the default signal for agents, covering tool calls and MCP calls.
Per-agent identity via SPIFFE/SPIRE is preferable to shared service accounts or human identities; egress network policy or proxying is the best value control.
Object capabilities: a proxy outside the micro VM holds the token and performs authentication, so the agent gets granular capabilities and no ambient credential.
Auditing requires tracing delegated authority through sub-agents; context propagation across A2A and MCP is hard to get right.

numbers.text: OpenAI reportedly spent about $1 million on tokens and found around 900 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
Running llm-d in production may need two clusters with about 250 GPUs each for redundancy.

open_gaps.text: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions have no stable release, and stabilizing them on top of fast-changing protocols is difficult.
Container isolation is not secure enough for agents, and sandboxing remains an unsolved cat-and-mouse problem.
SPIFFE/SPIRE gives fine-grained agent identity but has not become common because it is complex to deploy.
Getting started with agentic inference in production is much harder than with predictive inference, given GPU counts and redundancy.

opportunities.text: File issues on agent projects where trace context does not propagate correctly across A2A and MCP calls.
Put a credential-brokering proxy outside the agent sandbox so agents receive scoped capabilities instead of tokens.
Instrument agents from within using OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and use the traces to drive eval loops.
Pick a pet project that uses agents, tracing and the inference stack (vLLM, llm-d, Ray) end to end.

title: The Latest in GPU, TPU, NIC and Other Device Support - WG Device Management
tldr: WG Device Management reviewed what Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) shipped in Kubernetes 1.37 and what is landing in 1.38, from device taints and extended-resource compatibility to partitionable devices and CPU allocation through DRA. Next up are DRA preemption, gang-aware preemption, richer hardware models and attaching GPUs to running pods.

key_points.text: Device plugins expose an opaque integer count; the working group formed after KubeCon EU 2024 because AI ASICs, RDMA NICs and CXL memory need richer modeling.
DRA has four parts: ResourceSlice to describe devices, ResourceClaim to request them (including under-specified asks like any GPU with 20 GB), the scheduler match, and the kubelet/driver setup.
ResourceSlice is aimed at vendors, ResourceClaim at users and DeviceClass at admins, who can inject policy without changing user manifests.
1.37: extended resource requests let admins move to DRA drivers while users keep asking for nvidia.com/gpu-style resources.
1.37: device taints mark a single failing accelerator instead of tainting the whole node and stranding healthy devices.
1.37 began DRA integration with workload-aware scheduling: resource claims attach to a pod group, plus faster scheduling of many DRA pods at once.

1.38: partitionable devices (main case NVIDIA MIG), consumable capacity (for example sharing NIC bandwidth), and binding conditions that wait for slow fabric-attached devices and can reschedule on failure.

Node allocatable resources via DRA (beta in 1.38) let CPU, memory and hugepages be allocated in a claim and aligned with the NIC and GPU, with the scheduler avoiding double counting against the container spec.
With workload-aware scheduling, a claim per pod-group replica can allocate a compute domain or TPU slice and clean it up when the replica scales down.
Adoption needs vendors to ship drivers and ecosystem projects to consume DRA; Karpenter, Cluster Autoscaler and KubeVirt are integrating.
The DRA plugin is a default kube-scheduler plugin; most new DRA features have a scheduling component.

numbers.text: DRA went GA in Kubernetes 1.34; since 1.36 two to three DRA features graduate to GA each release.
About 20 active features are tracked by the working group at any time.
Placing a NIC and GPU on the same PCIe root can give about 10x the IO performance between them.

open_gaps.text: DRA does not yet support preemption; an alpha is targeted for 1.38, and gang-level (workload-aware) preemption comes later.
Attaching and detaching GPUs on running pods (in-place mutability) is early, possibly alpha in 1.39.
Components that make their own scheduling decisions, like Kueue and autoscalers, must understand DRA's programmable scheduling; shared importable libraries are being built.
No public fractional TPU sharing yet.

opportunities.text: Follow the working group's live feature tracking sheet and weekly meetings (EU- and US-friendly times).
Use a DeviceClass with extended resources to move a cluster to a DRA driver without changing user manifests.
Help autoscalers and admission controllers support newer DRA features such as partitionable devices.
Try DRA for non-traditional resources, such as locally cached models or NVMe access, as discussed in Q&A.

title: DisaggregatedSet Meets Multi-EPP: Coordinating llm-d at Scale in production
tldr: Mistral runs llm-d in production and contributed two pieces back: DisaggregatedSet, which manages prefill and decode as one unit inside LeaderWorkerSet, and a cross-replica syncer that lets several endpoint pickers share state so routing scales out.

key_points.text: Disaggregated serving splits compute-bound prefill from memory-bound decode for better service on the same GPUs, but it is hard to operate: rollouts can pair incompatible peers and break the prefill/decode ratio.
LeaderWorkerSet treats a multi-pod replica as one unit (if one pod dies, the group dies) and now supports gang scheduling.

DisaggregatedSet, now part of the LeaderWorkerSet project, declares prefill, decode (and encode) roles with topology-aware placement on NVL72 slices, coordinated progressive rollouts that hold the ratio, and per-role autoscaling.
Cross-revision gating: llm-d shifts traffic to a new revision gradually, only once compatible prefill and decode pods exist.
DisaggregatedSet has been a well-lit path since llm-d v1.
By default the EPP is active-passive: failover means downtime (fail closed) or poor routing (fail open), and the only way to grow is vertically.
Several EPPs without coordination drift apart, each seeing only part of the in-flight load.
The cross-replica syncer is a generic set/get interface; a plugin opts in with about 20 lines of Go by giving the state to sync and an aggregate function.
Mistral's Redis syncer runs every 50 ms in the background, so the request hot path never waits on Redis.

numbers.text: Rollouts happen several times a week.
At 300 RPS, three synced EPPs matched the cache hit rate of a single EPP with precise KV-aware routing.
Over 90% of measurements showed zero discrepancy between local and synced state at both 200 and 800 RPS.
One EPP broke down around 700 RPS; three synced EPPs kept serving.

open_gaps.text: Safer scale-up during rollouts is still landing (planned for DisaggregatedSet v1.1).
Redis transaction overhead grows with endpoints; a batched-set contribution is in review.
A peer-to-peer syncer that removes Redis entirely is in progress.

opportunities.text: Implement another cross-replica syncer backend, or help with the peer-to-peer one.
Run active-active EPPs with the Redis syncer and load-test past the ~700 RPS single-EPP limit.
Try DisaggregatedSet for prefill/decode rollouts instead of hand-managing two Deployments.
Explain why an active-passive router caps inference scale, using Mistral's numbers.

title: Why Are You Still Wasting Whole GPUs? Hardware-Level Sharing, Scheduled with DRA
tldr: A Pulumi solutions architect describes building a self-hosted inference platform for a European customer that splits GPUs into NVIDIA MIG slices and schedules them with Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). MIG gives the isolation time-slicing lacks, and DRA lets workloads ask for slices by attributes, but quotas, large models and chargeback remain open.

key_points.text: European customers want to self-host models for control and regulation; the speaker's view is that owning the model is easy and using the GPU well is hard.
Option one, one whole GPU per pod via the device plugin with vLLM, showed low utilization in Prometheus while the full card was paid for.
Option two, time-slicing, has no memory or fault isolation, so noisy neighbors hurt workloads; MPS has the same issue.
MIG gives slices with dedicated memory and cache and fault isolation between them; the number of slices depends on the card.
DRA mirrors the storage pattern (DeviceClass like StorageClass, claims like PVCs) and selects devices by attributes with CEL.
A shared ResourceClaim lets pods in a namespace share a device; a ResourceClaimTemplate gives each pod its own device matching a CEL selector.

The stack uses the NVIDIA DRA driver, which publishes MIG profiles as ResourceSlices, plus the Gateway API inference extension and agentgateway, which route by backend load instead of kube-proxy's blind balancing.
Demo on an AWS RTX instance: 1g, 2g and 4g MIG profiles exposed as slices; a Qwen3 server and a training pod each got their own slice, queried through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Rule of thumb: MIG for multiple tenants on one card, latency targets, or training and serving together; time-slicing is still fine for one trusted team, dev boxes and bursty jobs.
Rollout lessons: pick slice layouts per node pool, label pools with the MIG config, name slices clearly, and start DRA only after MIG is configured to avoid race conditions.
Guardrails at two points: policy as code in Pulumi before apply, and the same policy in Kyverno at the API server.

numbers.text: MIG slice counts cited: seven on larger data-center cards, four on the RTX card used in the demo.
A consumer RTX gaming GPU was quoted at about 9,000 euros.

open_gaps.text: Day-two questions are still open: MIG quota and ordering (a queue such as Kueue), group-shared claims in 1.37, admission policies, and llm-d as the next layer.
Models larger than a slice or a node need multi-node serving (LeaderWorkerSet is being evaluated); MoE models with prefill and decode pools still need investigation.
Chargeback to teams by slice-hours is the next big step and not yet built.

opportunities.text: Recreate the stack on one MIG-capable node: GPU driver, DRA driver, MIG profiles, and two workloads on separate slices behind an inference gateway.
Build slice-hour chargeback for MIG slices allocated through DRA.
Write a decision guide for MIG vs time-slicing vs MPS based on tenancy, isolation and burstiness.
Enforce GPU request policies both in CI and at the API server with Kyverno, so direct API access cannot bypass them.

title: Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent
tldr: Solo.io engineers tried a pod per agent, Anthropic's sandbox runtime, Agent Sandbox and NVIDIA OpenShell, and found each solved only part of the problem, so they joined Google's Agent Substrate and rebuilt kagent 1.0 on it. Their main lessons: isolation is table stakes, and the hard parts are suspend and resume, keeping all controls outside the agent, identity that follows the session, and treating snapshots as sensitive data.

key_points.text: An agent needs compute, identity, networking and storage like any workload, but sessions last hours, are stateful, mostly idle, and the agent can do anything a user can.
A sandbox defines what an agent can see, touch, call and persist: file system, network, tools, credentials, identity, and cleanup between sessions.
A homegrown pod per agent gave Kubernetes identity, policy and observability, but no real sandbox.

Anthropic's sandbox runtime (bubblewrap on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS, domain-allowlist proxy) suits laptops but meant many sandbox processes inside kagent pods, with no per-agent identity, a shared host kernel, and the proxy inside the sandbox.
Agent Sandbox gave a stateful pod under gVisor or Kata with sub-second warm pools, but idle agents still held CPU and memory and identity stayed with the pod.

NVIDIA OpenShell denied egress by default with per-binary rules and swapped placeholder credentials for real keys at the proxy, but still ran one always-on sandbox per agent with enforcement inside it.
Agent Substrate snapshots idle actors to object storage, restores them in milliseconds, keeps the Kubernetes API off the hot path, and is default-deny with no keys inside.

kagent 1.0 is rebuilt on Agent Substrate: a harness (owned by infra), an agent template, and an agent binding them, compiled into an actor template; each session becomes an actor reachable over A2A, MCP or gRPC.
A new sandbox template resource defines the OCI image, preloaded directories, git repos and skills; one user's agents began sharing state through a common sandbox file system on their own.

Lessons: all controls live outside the agent, identity follows the actor not the pod, suspended agents are stored data that need encryption, retention and restore rules, and the sandbox runtime becomes part of the snapshot format.
Demo: Anthropic-hosted managed agents run sessions in kagent sandboxes on your cluster; file systems are isolated per session and egress is denied until a policy is applied at runtime.

numbers.text: Agent Sandbox warm pools start a pod in under a second.
Agent Substrate restores actors from snapshots in milliseconds, versus seconds for pods.

open_gaps.text: kagent has not enabled memory snapshots because of their complexity, and the runtime-specific snapshot format needs to be hidden from most users.
Managed-agent support (provider-hosted loop, local sandboxes) is experimental and on main only; the team wants feedback on whether it belongs in kagent core.
Snapshotting GPU state so inference can run inside the same actors is still being worked on.
Agents sharing a sandbox file system to talk to each other was an emergent, probably insecure behavior.

opportunities.text: Compare where egress and credential enforcement live in Anthropic's sandbox runtime, OpenShell, Agent Sandbox and Agent Substrate.
Encrypt agent snapshot buckets and define retention and who may restore a session.
Try the experimental managed-agent support in kagent main and report whether it should be in core.
Define kagent sandbox templates with default-deny egress and add allow rules dynamically per agent.

title: Platform-First AI Agent Security: Zero-Trust Patterns for Kubernetes
tldr: Carlos Santana argues platform teams should treat AI agents as untrusted tenants and layer identity, policy and isolation around them using CNCF projects. He shows KRO compositions that stamp out agent workloads, egress policies and Agent Substrate worker pools per namespace, plus Agent Sandbox warm pools, OpenShell with Cedar policies, and credential proxies.

key_points.text: Enterprise interest in agent security is driven by insecure agent use and incidents where agents reach systems they should not, not by productivity.
Treat agents as tenants running untrusted, LLM-generated code; the three concerns are identity, policy and isolation.

Identity has two cases: an agent acting for an interactive user (token exchange) and an agent running overnight without the user; SPIFFE/SPIRE gives agents a URI identity tied to a JWT or X.509 certificate.

Policy covers what an agent may run and read, including layer 7 paths, plus temporal rules (e.g. deny after five executions) via Dogwood, an AWS project built on Cedar, using audit logs of agent sessions.
A KRO resource graph definition declares a CRD and its controller in YAML with CEL, so platform teams can define an AgentWorkload with a narrow prompt and allowed FQDNs without writing Go.
The AgentWorkload composes an egress policy, an agent template and an agent, the kagent abstractions now built on Agent Substrate; KRO infers creation order from references.
A new experimental KRO graph mode creates a worker pool, harness, service account and quota in any namespace labeled as a tenant; resource quotas can cap custom resources such as agents.
Owning your own platform APIs shields consumers from breaking changes in fast-moving agent projects.
Isolation levels: gVisor syscall emulation, VM isolation with Kata Containers, and hardware isolation with the newly announced AWS Nitro Sandboxes on EKS.
Agent Sandbox warm pools with claims (like PVCs) hand out a ready sandbox instantly and backfill the pool.

OpenShell restricts which files and binaries an agent can use; an open PR proposes Cedar as its policy language, e.g. allowing GitHub access only through one binary. Secrets are injected by a credential proxy, never given to the agent.

numbers.text: Launching a micro VM takes three to four seconds, plus a couple of seconds for the image.
A claim against a warm pool returns a sandbox in under a second.
The KRO graph feature arrived this week in KRO 0.10 and is experimental.

open_gaps.text: Cedar as OpenShell's policy language is still an open proposal and PR, not merged.
The KRO graph mode is experimental and needs user feedback.
Handling permissions for agents that run overnight without the user is an open identity question.
Agent behavior cannot be pinpointed in advance, so policy must describe expected behavior rather than exact actions.

opportunities.text: Define a KRO-based AgentWorkload API that bundles egress policy, agent template and quota, so teams consume a stable platform interface.
Put a credential proxy in front of agents that injects secrets into outbound requests instead of mounting them.
Review the Cedar policy proposal for OpenShell and give feedback on KRO's experimental graph mode.
Compare gVisor, Kata Containers and hardware-isolated micro VMs for running untrusted agent code.

title: The Scheduling Stack: Real-World Lessons from Anthropic, Anyscale, Google, and CERN
tldr: Big AI users still outgrow the default Kubernetes scheduler, so upstream is turning the scheduling stack into pluggable parts. The hard problems now are fragmentation, multi-cluster onboarding and failures, not raw node count.

key_points.text: Anthropic ran the default kube-scheduler for three years with node selectors and scheduling gates, then built its own about two years ago when gang and topology needs outgrew it.
Anyscale is excited about pod groups and the new Workload API; RL post-training mixes training, inference and data processing in one job.

Google's view: the scheduler is a framework with sane defaults for most users, and every layer (placement, queueing such as Kueue, hardware programming like GPU compute domains or TPU slices, autoscaling) should be replaceable on its own.
CERN runs multi-cluster for capacity, not scale: any team or HPC site that hands over a Kubernetes API endpoint gets onboarded, including GPUs 100 m underground at ALICE.
At Anthropic, cross-cluster pain is above Kubernetes: namespaces, service accounts, RBAC and data locality in each cluster.
The real limit is workload count and churn, not nodes. Keep one tightly coupled workload in one cluster; use many clusters for many workloads.
Fragmentation: Anyscale mixes high-priority training with preemptible batch; Anthropic blocks fragmentation at placement and runs a background defrag job. No silver bullet.
Small workloads that do not fill a node or GPU need attention; CERN published a CNCF reference architecture for it.
Multi-layer schedulers (Ray on Kubernetes) need better vertical building blocks; the API server and etcd watch path adds latency no fast scheduler can remove.

numbers.text: Anthropic and Google pushed one cluster to 65,000 nodes.
CERN runs 5,000-node clusters.
Minor scheduler and component tuning for sub-node workloads gave CERN about 30% better performance.

open_gaps.text: The default scheduler still does not meet frontier-lab needs; pluggability is 'not there yet'.
Kubernetes was designed for single-cluster scheduling; multi-cluster needs extra layers each user builds.
Generic checkpoint and restore for non-ML, long-running scientific jobs is still being worked out.
No standard building blocks to integrate application schedulers (Ray) with Kubernetes scheduling.

opportunities.text: Follow the Workload API / pod groups work in SIG Scheduling; it is the upstream answer to gang scheduling.
Show priority plus preemptible batch sharing one GPU pool (for example with Kueue and Karpenter) and measure cost saved.
Compare in-placement anti-fragmentation rules vs background defrag for GPU clusters, using this panel's two approaches.
Apply CERN's sub-node scheduling reference architecture on another platform and report the result back.

title: Clueless About The Cost of AI Model Usage? OpenCost+llm-d = first of a kind inference cost tracking
tldr: OpenCost now reads llm-d and vLLM token metrics and combines them with provider pricing and DCGM data to report cost per model and per token. A live demo on an IBM research cluster compares allocation and usage cost to expose idle models, and the roadmap targets GPU usage-based allocation, time slicing and richer idle detection.

key_points.text: Self-hosted models are generally cheaper than hosted ones, but that only delays the cost problem as self-hosting grows.
OpenCost, a CNCF incubating FinOps tool, covers Kubernetes, cloud provider and plugin-based SaaS costs via the FOCUS spec, with Parquet exporters, APIs and a UI.
Responsibility split: llm-d handles token counts, routing and scheduling; OpenCost handles pricing, cloud provider connections and metric aggregation, and never runs LLMs.
Outputs include dollars per token and hardware utilization, aimed at cost-aware model routing and comparing self-hosting with hosted APIs.
Allocation cost is the max of request and usage, a production metric that rewards right-sizing; usage cost charges only measured use, an R&D metric that tolerates over-requesting.
Input versus output cost is split using vLLM prefill time versus decode time.
Demo: the inference-cost totals API aggregated by model and namespace showed a large gap between allocation and usage cost for one model, marking it for right-sizing or more traffic.
Per-model idle cost is derived from two OpenCost API calls, one sharing idle and shared costs and one keeping them separate, then subtracting.
Dashboard widgets show cost per million tokens and the most idle and most expensive idle models; many models had no tokens, like abandoned container workloads.

numbers.text: OpenCost launched in 2019 and has about 7,000 GitHub stars.
A CNCF survey found 66% of AI workloads run on Kubernetes.
Worked example: $1 per vCPU-hour, $10 per GPU-hour, $15 total over 150 tokens gives 10 cents per token.
Demo cluster: several dozen llm-d deployments on a few dozen H100 nodes.
One 120B model over 24 hours: $246 allocation cost ($239 input, $7 output) versus about $22 usage cost.
That model was idle 90% of the time.
The most efficient models were only 39% idle; one idle model cost almost $24K over a week.

open_gaps.text: GPU allocation uses only resource requests; usage metrics still need to be folded in, and GPU time slicing is not supported yet.
Idle detection relies on a single DCGM metric; memory, PCIe and other GPU dimensions are needed to judge fit and right-sizing.
KV cache settings exist in the API but are not tightly integrated yet.
OpenCost has no native per-model idle view, so it is computed with a two-call workaround.

opportunities.text: Use allocation-versus-usage cost per model to find idle or abandoned LLM deployments and right-size them.
Help OpenCost add GPU time slicing and multi-metric GPU idle detection.
Prototype cost-aware model routing that consumes OpenCost cost-per-token metrics.
Compare self-hosted dollars per token from this integration with hosted API pricing for the same workload.

title: Reduce vLLM Pod Cold Starts with KServe Kernel Caching
tldr: Even with model weights cached, each new vLLM pod recompiles its GPU kernels. KServe now captures those compiled artifacts, publishes them as signed OCI images, and lets new pods reuse them, cutting compile time from about 35 seconds to about 1 second in their tests.

key_points.text: KServe turns a ServingRuntime and an InferenceService into a Deployment; a storage initializer downloads the model, then vLLM loads it and initializes before the pod is ready.
vLLM startup steps: model loading, graph compilation, CUDA graph capture, and engine initialization (memory profiling, KV cache allocation).
A new replica on another node does not inherit compiled artifacts and repeats every startup step. Model download can be avoided with KServe's local model cache; kernel compilation is the focus here.

Compiling at runtime fits the code to the actual GPU architecture, tensor shapes, data types and vLLM/PyTorch/CUDA versions. vLLM already saves compiled artifacts to a cache directory, but ephemeral pod storage loses them.
Shared NFS (ReadWriteMany) adds a storage dependency during burst scale-out, and node-local caches must be copied between nodes. Since the cache is executable code, its origin must be trusted.
The approach: package compiled artifacts as an OCI image, push to a registry, sign it, verify the signature before reuse, and prefetch onto GPU nodes.
This began as a separate GPU Kernel Manager (GKM) project using persistent volumes; in KServe it moved to OCI images for portability and signing. The feature is optional.

Cache selection uses a workload footprint (workload, runtime image, model) and a compatibility footprint (data type, compile settings). It prefers the same workload, then a compatible one, else compiles and captures a new cache.
vLLM logs confirmed the precompiled AOT artifacts were loaded, so the gain came from real cache reuse.

On a fresh GPU node, pulling the runtime image took longer than the rest of vLLM startup after cache reuse. Next idea: prefetch the runtime image and kernel cache onto new GPU nodes ahead of time (not yet measured end to end).
Q&A: unlike GPU snapshotting, this needs no special device or fast GPU-to-GPU network; it uses OCI images, registries and cosign with cert-manager, and works in disconnected clusters.

numbers.text: Baseline vLLM startup is about 250 seconds, excluding image pull and model download.
Model loading takes about 142 seconds (57%), compilation 35 seconds (14%), CUDA graph capture 12 seconds, 52 seconds of bootstrap and 9 seconds of API startup.
Test setup: Qwen2.5 32B with AWQ quantization on an NVIDIA L40S GPU.
Cache capture added no penalty: about 160 seconds versus 169 seconds for local model alone.
With cache reuse, startup dropped from 160 to 110 seconds and compile time from about 35 to 1.16 seconds, a 96% reduction.
Engine initialization dropped from about 55 to 18 seconds.
Full pod startup on a fresh GPU node was about 11 minutes standard and about 3 minutes with a local model; model loading to GPU still took 128 seconds.
Pulling the runtime image on a new GPU node took about 157 seconds.

open_gaps.text: Model loading into GPU memory remains the largest startup cost and is not addressed by kernel caching.
Runtime image pull on new GPU nodes can exceed the remaining startup time; image prefetch is proposed but not measured end to end.
Changing compilation options invalidates the cached image, so the cache must be rebuilt.

opportunities.text: Measure your full cold start by stage (image pull, download, loading, compile, CUDA graphs) before choosing what to cache.
Enable KServe kernel caching with signed OCI artifacts alongside local model caching for vLLM services that scale out often.
Prefetch runtime images and kernel caches onto new GPU nodes before pods are scheduled.
Compare kernel caching with GPU snapshotting for cold starts, covering hardware requirements and trust.

title: Deep Dive Into the DRA Driver for NVIDIA GPUs: What Works Today, What’s Coming and Why It Matters
tldr: NVIDIA's DRA driver for GPUs already handles time-slicing, MPS, MIG, VM passthrough, health-based device taints and multi-node NVLink through compute domains. The next release adds cross-namespace GPU sharing, several compute-domain pods per node, an always-on IMEX daemon set and beta graduation of most driver features.

key_points.text: The driver has a GPU kubelet plugin, a compute-domain kubelet plugin and a compute-domain controller; it ships as a Helm chart, with features such as MIG and passthrough behind feature gates.

GPU Operator adds a new GPUCluster API that deploys the DRA plugins, DCGM, the DCGM exporter and a validator; it drops the NVIDIA container runtime in favor of CDI and gives monitoring pods admin-access claims.
The GPU Operator DRA mode does not support mixed clusters with the device plugin yet; migration support is planned for an upcoming release.

Sharing today is user-mediated: pods share one ResourceClaim within a namespace. The next release adds system-mediated sharing across namespaces using consumable capacity, with admin-set share counts and no oversubscription.
NVML health events become device taints so the scheduler avoids bad GPUs; next, the DRA resource health status API will show the XID error in pod status.
KubeVirt VMs request a VFIO device class; the driver switches the GPU to the VFIO driver and the DRA downward API tells the VM launcher which GPU it got.
Each GPU is published as both a container device and a VFIO device with the same PCI bus ID; allocating one hides the other, and the partitionable devices API will make this accounting native.
Compute domains run IMEX for multi-node NVLink; today each node allows only channel 0 and one pod, which must take all four GPUs.

Next release: multiple compute-domain pods per node with unique channels, a ComputeDomainDaemonSet that keeps IMEX running ahead of workloads with clique-by-clique rolling updates, and NVLink between pods on one node, including HGX.
Demo: a device taint rule with NoExecute simulated an XID failure and the compute-domain workload moved to another node.
Migration: nvidia.com/gpu requests are turned into DRA claims for full GPUs and MIG (MIG needs a device class per profile); time-sliced and MPS requests cannot be translated yet.

numbers.text: KubeVirt 1.9 added beta support for DRA GPU resources.
Demo node had four GB200 GPUs shared between VMs and pods.
Most Kubernetes DRA feature gates the driver relies on moved to beta in 1.36.

open_gaps.text: Driver features for GPU sharing, health checking and passthrough are still alpha; beta is planned for the next release.
No straightforward migration from device-plugin time-slicing or MPS to DRA yet.
Bootstrapping IMEX daemons per workload adds latency at scale, which the daemon set is meant to fix.
vGPU support is coming next, with MIG-backed vGPU in a later release.

opportunities.text: On Kubernetes 1.36 or later, try moving nvidia.com/gpu workloads to DRA via extended-resource translation, starting with full GPUs and MIG.
Run VMs and containers on the same GPU nodes using the VFIO device class and KubeVirt.
Test the upcoming ComputeDomainDaemonSet and multi-pod compute domains and send feedback to the driver maintainers.
Document topology alignment between the GPU DRA driver and DRANET or the SR-IOV DRA driver for RDMA setups.

title: Governing and Scaling Agents in Heterogeneous Environments
tldr: Antonio Ojea and Tomás Tormo present Agent Mesh, a network for agents running on Kubernetes, laptops, VMs and serverless, built on a libp2p peer-to-peer data plane with Kademlia discovery. Policy travels with each node as signed, attenuable Biscuit tokens minted at enrollment, and a live hospital demo shows label-based rules keeping EU data in the EU.

key_points.text: Regulated customers run agents on laptops, VMs and serverless as well as Kubernetes, and cannot replace existing platforms, so a Kubernetes-only answer creates silos.
The solution must run as an SDK, a sidecar or a gateway and work with existing open protocols.
A VPN does not fit: it gives L3/L4 connectivity with IPAM pain and no visibility, and a compromised agent gets open access.
Agent traffic falls into five kinds: LLM calls, tools over MCP, agent-to-agent (A2A), external apps such as GitHub, and services the agent exposes.
Data plane: libp2p over a Kademlia DHT, with a cryptographic identity per node, TLS between nodes and built-in service discovery.
Policy: webhooks and Lua/Wasm extensions are opaque and fragile, so they chose Biscuit, signed tokens with a Datalog policy language, exposed to admins through a simpler DSL.
The control plane connects to an external identity provider, compiles policy to Datalog and mints a Biscuit at enrollment. Biscuits work offline, so connected nodes no longer need the control plane.
Biscuit blocks can only attenuate, so a node can narrow delegated rights, for example to one MCP tool or one HTTP path.
Nodes set label requirements for inbound and outbound peers (for example region EU), checked in a five-step exchange before any data flows.
Architecture: control plane, admin-run routers that keep the Kademlia network up, and nodes or embedded SDKs; one binary bundles control plane, router and console.
Demo: the US diagnoser is refused by the laptop's EU-only egress rule, and the model cannot override it because the node enforces it; a banned phone is cut off after the control plane notifies peers.

numbers.text: A new mesh can be created in about 10 seconds using a tunnel broker.
Five categories of agent traffic: LLM, MCP tools, A2A, external apps, exposed services.
A five-step check runs between nodes before any data flows.
Agent Mesh v0.2.0 was just released.

open_gaps.text: Schema-based filtering of MCP traffic is hard to maintain when there can be millions of tools and fields change often.
Region rules depend on admins labeling nodes correctly; the mesh only enforces the labels it is given.
Next: connecting HPC centers and cloud providers to run workflows, with Lawrence Livermore National Lab, and closer work with the A2A protocol.

opportunities.text: Biscuit tokens: offline verification, Datalog policies and attenuation for delegating narrower rights to sub-agents.
Enforce data residency for agent traffic with signed node labels and egress requirements instead of prompt instructions.
Create a mesh or join the public testnet and connect agents across a laptop, a VM and a cluster.
Help with Agent Mesh's A2A integration or new SDK and platform integrations.

title: Inside the Inference Load Balancer: Proxy/Controller Patterns for LLM Serving on Kubernetes
tldr: OpenAI's inference load balancer picks a GPU engine for every request across clusters and regions. A global control plane computes routing weights from demand, capacity and latency profiles; fast local data planes apply them, with penalties, retry caps and load shedding for protection.

key_points.text: The load balancer runs in CPU front-end clusters and proxies requests to inference engines in GPU clusters; both sides run on Kubernetes.

The least-busy engine is not always fastest: one that already caches the conversation reaches the first token sooner. Signals are TTFT, time between output tokens, load, errors, network latency and cache affinity.
The balancer itself is plain Kubernetes: Deployments, HPA on CPU and custom metrics, readiness probes, and GPU cluster locations from a ConfigMap.
Early design: filter eligible engines (capabilities, data location), then weighted consistent hashing, with weights nudged by a proportional feedback loop.
That design was hard to explain, unbalanced across GPU generations, and weight shifts broke cache affinity, causing oscillation.
Current design copies Kubernetes' control/data plane split (like kube-proxy and EndpointSlices): each data plane routes from locally cached weights, never calling the control plane per request.
Nearest-engine routing fails because demand and GPU capacity are not balanced by region; a farther engine can win end to end.
The optimizer takes per-cluster demand, network latency, engine capacity and health, and latency-vs-load profiles, and minimizes expected end-to-end latency subject to capacity limits.
Protection: outlier penalties, bounded retries (retries are costly because the new engine lacks the cache), and load shedding as a last resort.
Q&A: spiky API traffic uses other algorithms, more headroom and wider destination pools; uncached tokens are the work measure; each model version is routed as its own model.

numbers.text: Optimized routing weights cut network overhead by about 40%.
Example: a cluster sending 120 RPS to a 100 RPS engine nearby, while another region uses only 40 of 80 RPS.

open_gaps.text: Bursty API traffic against lagging state can still overload a few engines.
Retry caps that suit normal load can be too high during fleet-wide overload.
Persistent engine faults still need manual investigation and vendor follow-up.

opportunities.text: Compare this control/data plane design with llm-d's endpoint picker and Gateway API inference routing.
Prototype a global routing-weight optimizer for multi-region inference, with latency-vs-load profiles per engine.
Add cache-aware retry budgets and load shedding to your inference gateway.
Proportional and PID control, and why mixing many signals into one weight oscillates.

title: Securing the Agentic Future: Distributing LLM Weights and Sandboxed AI Agents via Harbor
tldr: An AI agent ships as two things, model weights and the sandbox it acts in, and today neither goes through the supply chain teams already use for container images. The talk shows Harbor storing weights as ModelPack OCI artifacts and agent images with a sandbox permission descriptor, so both get the same scanning, signing, replication and admission policy.

key_points.text: An agent is a model, instructions, a runtime loop and tools; five of those six pieces already ship as OCI images, but model weights are usually loose Hugging Face files with no digest or signature.

Typical practice: weights downloaded onto a VM, PVC or S3 bucket with no revision pinning or scanning, which fails outright in air-gapped clusters; agent tools are pulled from the internet at runtime with no policy.
Target state: one registry (Harbor) and two artifact types, models as ModelPack artifacts and agents plus tools as plain OCI images, inside one trust boundary.

ModelPack (CNCF sandbox) defines a model as an OCI artifact: a model config with architecture, parameters, precision and license, plus typed layers for weights, tokenizer config and docs. The modctl CLI builds, pushes and pulls them like Docker.
Spec recommendations: one weight file per layer so parallel and P2P pulls work, and leave weights uncompressed because gzip gains nothing on near-random data.

Harbor shows model metadata natively and adds Hugging Face model sync: register an endpoint and token, create a sync policy, and Harbor pulls a revision and republishes it as ModelPack. It is model-aware sync, not a proxy cache.
Once in Harbor, models get a model scanner (e.g. flagging pickle files that run code on load), SBOMs, Cosign signing and a rule to refuse unsigned artifacts.
Distribution: a central Harbor replicates to regional Harbors, and Dragonfly P2P lets nodes share per-file layers so the registry serves a model once.
