Pods mount the model with Kubernetes image volumes, pinned by digest; admission policy must cover image volumes, not just containers. The demo synced a model from Hugging Face and served it from a Harbor-backed image volume.

Docker's experimental sandbox kit spec attaches a descriptor to the agent image listing allowed network destinations, credentials and writable paths; pinning the agent by digest also pins its permissions.
Admission then allows registry pulls only from Harbor, verifies signatures on agent and model, and the sandbox enforces egress to only Harbor and the inference server.

open_gaps.text: The sandbox kit spec has no final version yet, and today only Docker's sandbox runtime reads the descriptor.
ModelPack support in Harbor is still a community proposal targeted at the next release.
Each agent tool (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor) defines what an agent may touch in its own way, outside the artifact.

opportunities.text: Package model weights with modctl as ModelPack artifacts and mount them in pods via digest-pinned image volumes instead of init-container downloads.
Extend admission policy to verify signatures on image volumes and restrict model and agent pulls to your own registry.
Review the Harbor ModelPack proposal and help sandbox runtimes adopt the sandbox kit descriptor once it is donated to CNCF.
Model-specific scanning risks such as pickle files that execute code on load, which CVE scanners miss.

title: Who Ran Up the Inference Bill? AI Traffic Control with KServe and Gateway API Inference Extensions
tldr: A beginner-level talk on attributing and controlling inference spend by putting an AI-aware gateway in front of KServe models. A live demo on kind uses agentgateway with the Gateway API Inference Extension to log tokens per team, enforce per-team token budgets, block sensitive data and fail over to a cloud LLM.

key_points.text: Inference bills show a total but not which team or service spent the tokens, and request counts mislead because token use per request varies widely.
Inference traffic differs from classic traffic: seconds to minutes, streamed token by token, costly, routed on the body, so request limits and round-robin balancing stop working.
KServe creates the HTTPRoute, InferencePool and endpoint picker from one model resource.
The endpoint picker chooses pods using KV cache, prefix and LoRA adapter state instead of load alone.
Any gateway that supports the Inference Extension works; the demo uses agentgateway as the AI-aware gateway.
Local models need a cost too; a rough GPU-hours-over-tokens figure is enough to visualize spend.
Plain Gateway API logs show only status codes; with the inference extension, logs include input and output tokens and the model.
Per-team traffic showed the team with the fewest requests spent the most tokens.
A guardrail rejected a prompt containing a credit card number at the gateway; a team past its token budget got 429s while other teams kept working.
When the local model returned 500, the gateway failed over to a cloud LLM without interrupting users.
Takeaways: meter tokens not requests, put a name on every token, control spend at the gateway, build on standards and keep policy thin.

numbers.text: Example per-team budget: 60,000 tokens, after which requests get HTTP 429.
Mock LLM log entry: 6 input tokens, 1 output token.
The ML research team sent only 3 requests but spent the most tokens.

open_gaps.text: Per-token cost for self-hosted models is a rough estimate, not a production calculation.
Classic request limits and round-robin load balancing do not fit token-based inference traffic.
Standard Gateway API logs carry no token or model data without an inference-aware gateway.

opportunities.text: Add per-team token budgets and failover to a cloud model at your AI gateway.
Run the speaker's kind-based demo repo with KServe and agentgateway.
Export gateway token logs to your monitoring stack to split the inference bill by team.
Join the KServe CNCF Slack or the agentgateway Discord to work on AI gateway features.

title: The Seams Are the Trap: Agent Fleets from CNCF Parts You Already Have
tldr: IBM speakers built a headless agent fleet from existing CNCF parts: KEDA scales agent runners from Kafka lag, CloudEvents carry the tasks, and a small Python glue layer bridges HTTP and Kafka. Events are signed and kept in order, so the Kafka log doubles as a verifiable audit trail, while agent identity with SPIFFE/SPIRE is still unsolved.

key_points.text: Premise: instead of buying an agent platform, compose components many clusters already run (KEDA, Kafka via Strimzi, CloudEvents) and add only thin glue code.
KEDA scales on consumer lag, the work left in a Kafka topic, so agent runners scale to zero when idle; cooldown settings stop scale-down from flapping.

Their added parts: an event bridge that turns HTTP requests into Kafka events and Kafka events back into notifications, and event runners that consume tasks, start agents and publish agent output back to Kafka.
Events are signed when the bridge accepts them; the runner checks the signature and that the agent may consume the event before it starts the agent.
Kafka keeps the signed event sequence, so the log works as an audit trail that can show lost or injected events. The last event of a run, the terminal event, records the result.
Kafka partitions keep events in order per consumer, which suits stateful, long-running agents that receive several inputs.
Runs are labeled as groups so a batch of many agents produces one start and one finish notification instead of one per agent.
Demo: Claude Code in headless mode, using an event bridge skill, submits one task and then a batch of 100. Results arrive on a phone through ntfy with an HTML view of the run.
The audit tool verifies signatures and terminal events; an unsigned event injected directly into Kafka is rejected by the agent runner.
Everything is in Python, with specifications in their GitHub repo so it can be rebuilt in another language.
Q&A: not an anti-vendor talk; the speaker expects pluggable library pieces on top of KEDA and Kafka rather than one sold platform.

numbers.text: Demo batch of 100 agents across 12 Kafka partitions, with KEDA capped at 10 runner pods.
A single agent run produced 16 events, mostly internal Claude events.
The task lifecycle in the demo has seven steps, from submission to scale back to zero.
Scaling back down after the batch took about two to three minutes.

open_gaps.text: SPIFFE/SPIRE ties identity to a pod, but an agent's identity shifts as it gains skills and plugins at runtime; they have only a simple workaround.
Changing who may consume events is not dynamic: runners are scaled to zero and reconfigured.
KEDA scale-up is not instant, so large batches wait while runners start.

opportunities.text: Put signed CloudEvents and signature checks in front of agents you trigger from a queue, and verify the event log as an audit trail.
Scale headless agent workers from queue lag with KEDA, including scale to zero.
Work on dynamic agent identity that reflects loaded skills and plugins, beyond pod-level SPIFFE IDs.
Kafka partitions, consumer offsets and lag, and how they give ordering and crash recovery for agent tasks.
